(p-384) Surah al-Ankabut (The Spider)

Its purpose is to urge diligent striving in enjoining what is good, forbidding what is evil, and calling to Allah Most High and praising Him without slackening, just as the preceding surah ended with that, without turning aside at all to anything other than Him, glory be to Him, lest the example of relief for one who takes something else in exchange be like the example of the spider. So it is a surah on the weakness of the disbelievers and the strength of the believers. The secret of its being named "The Spider" has become clear, and that it points to its purpose. "In the name of Allah" (Bismillah), who encompasses all power, so He strengthens His soldiers; "the Most Merciful" (al-Rahman), who includes all servants with the blessing of commanding and forbidding; "the Most Compassionate" (al-Rahim), who obliges the people of recognition (al-'irfan) to the pinnacle of excellence (ihsan).

When He concluded the preceding surah with urging action for the Hereafter, and that every person, whether a doer of good or evil, is recompensed according to his deeds, and with the information that He, glory be to Him, knows the secret and the open, with the command to strive diligently in calling to Him and to direct aspirations toward Him, even if that leads to weariness and the loss of self and wealth, giving as the reason that the sovereignty is His, glory be to Him, because He is the Everlasting without cessation, while everything other than Him is toward perishing and dissolution, and that nothing escapes Him in any state or outcome, He began this surah with: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾, indicating by the alif, which denotes the Supreme Self-Subsisting Who encompasses all, and the lam of connection, and the mim of completeness, (p-385) by way of symbol, that He, glory be to Him, sent Gabriel to Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon them both, to call people to Allah by means of the Qur'an which was enjoined upon him, so that by the call their inner states are made known, and by the obligation those who are sincere are distinguished from those who are deceitful: ﴿And We will surely test you until We know those among you who strive and the steadfast, and We will test your reports﴾ [Muhammad: 31].

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 2:

When he expressed himself with this allusion for people of insight and perceptive hearts, he said, rebuking those who thought that one who claims faith is not tested with proof, and detailing what this surah was concluded with from all these meanings, building upon what the letters indicated for those possessed of gnosis: ﴿Do people think﴾ that is, all of them, for each of them claims that he is a believer, in the sense that he says: he is upon the truth. Perhaps he expressed it with "thinking" (husban) and "wavering" (nawas) as an indication that the doer of this is disturbed in intellect and deviant in temperament.

Since "thinking" (husban) cannot be linked to single nouns, but is linked only to the content of a clause, and since the intended meaning is to deny the thought of mere abandonment, "an" (that) was a verbal particle (masdariyyah) according to all the readers. So he expressed the content of something like: that He would leave them untested for their saying "we believe," by his saying: ﴿that they be left﴾ that is, at some time, in some way. Had he put the verb in the nominative, it would have conveyed that what is denied is the thought of confirmed abandonment, and then it would not serve to deny what is free of it. What benefits here has already passed in al-Ma'idah. ﴿That﴾ that is, that (p-386) ﴿they say﴾ even if that were in the sense of renewal and continuity: ﴿"We believe," and they﴾ that is, while they ﴿are not tested﴾ that is, their testing occurs from Him to whom belongs the whole affair and to whom belongs the greatness in the heavens and the earth, time after time, by testing the soundness of their saying first by sending the messengers, sending down the books and establishing the rulings, and second by patience over hardship and adversity when they encounter those who are called to God, in bearing their harm and swallowing their afflictions and other such acts, by which the rank of sayings is known, in soundness and in corruption.

Imam Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: The surah of al-Qasas opened with mention of the testing of the Children of Israel by Pharaoh, his slaughter of their sons, and their patience under the great ordeal. Then He, exalted, mentioned the good outcome of their affair and the fruit of their patience. Along with that, there came in what is from it, but separated from its generality by the matter of the mother of Moses: her trial by separation from him in infancy at the beginning of nursing, and her patience over the painful taste of that, until He returned him to her in the most beautiful and best return. Then He mentioned the trial of Moses, peace be upon him, by the matter of the Copt, his going out fearful and watching, and the good end and great mercy of his affair. All of this is a trial that brought forth good. It was concluded with mercy. Then came another kind of trial that brought an ordeal, produced evil and a bad temptation: the trial of Qarun with his wealth and his being seduced by it, so We caused the earth to swallow him and his home. Thereby it results that testing in (p-387) the greater part of the matter is a sunnah, and it proceeds from Him, glorified be He, among His servants, so that He may distinguish the wicked from the good. He is exempt from needing to learn the states of His servants through what He tests them with, since it is known that this occurs from them before it occurs, for He is their creator and originator, good or evil. How then could anything be hidden from Him, or would He need to make clear to Himself the states of the servants, or would His knowledge depend on a cause? ﴿Does not He who created know, and He is the Subtle, the Aware?﴾ [al-Mulk: 14]. Rather, it is a sunnah among His servants, so that there may become manifest among some of them to others, at the time of temptation and trial, what would not have become manifest before that, until they bear witness against themselves, and the proof is established against them by their own acknowledgment. He, exalted, has no need of any of that. When the surah of al-Qasas contained this testing in good and evil, and with it its opening and closing occurred, and it has accomplished, by the indication of the allusion, first the departure of our Prophet (ﷺ) from his land and place of origin, so that he, peace be upon him, would take the fullest share of what the messengers and prophets were tested with, of separation from homeland and what secures for them the reward befitting the loftiness of their ranks, peace be upon them; then, lastly, the glad tidings to him (ﷺ) of return and victory: ﴿Indeed, He who ordained the Qur'an for you will surely return you to a place of return﴾ [al-Qasas: 85]. Then He, glorified be He, followed this by his saying, informing the servants and alerting them that this is His sunnah among them. So He said: ﴿Do people think that they will be left to say "we believe" and they will not be tested?﴾ that is: do they think that mere acceptance and outward repentance will be sufficient for them, (p-388) and that they will not be tested with hardships and difficulties and various kinds of trials? ﴿And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and loss of wealth and lives and fruits﴾ [al-Baqarah: 155]. When the trial occurs, there is a group who receive it as one who knows that it is from God as a trial and test, so it becomes a refining and purification for them; and there is a group who meet it with the pleasure of Satan and hastening toward disbelief and abandonment: ﴿And whoever strives, he strives only for himself﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 6]. Then He, glorified be He, followed this by mentioning the state of some people who claim faith: when some small harm from the disbelievers reaches them, that turns them away from their faith, and they regard the punishment of God, which deters those who strike them from disbelief and opposition, as opposing them. So He, exalted, said: ﴿And among people is one who says, "We believe in God," but when he is harmed for the sake of God, he regards the trial of people as the punishment of God﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 10]. So what then is the state of these people in receiving what is greater than that trial and more severe in ordeal? Then He, glorified be He, followed that with what the one who is granted success consoles himself with: the patience of the prophets, peace be upon them, and the long struggle they endured from their peoples. He mentioned Noah, Abraham, Lot and Shu'ayb, peace be upon them, and singled these out for mention because they were among the greatest of the messengers in struggle and the most severely tested. As for Noah, peace be upon him, he remained among his people, as God the Exalted informed, a thousand years less fifty years, and none believed with him except a few. As for Abraham, peace be upon him, he was thrown with the catapult into the fire, and it became cool and safe for him. The Mighty Book has explicitly stated concerning those mentioned, peace be upon them, various kinds of trials, which they obtained the reward of, and they attained through them the great prophetic rank in its highest and most excellent standing. Then God, exalted, mentioned the seizing of the deniers from their nations, so He said: ﴿So each We seized for his sin﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 40]. Then He enjoined His Prophet (ﷺ) and clarified His proof, and the coherence of the speech continued to the end of the surah. End.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 3:

Since patient endurance (al-ta'assi) is one of the customary ways of human beings, the addressee who hears this command anticipates information about their condition in this matter. So He said, emphasizing it for the one who thinks that trial (al-ibtila') does not happen, because God is free of need for it, so there is no benefit in it, being ignorant of the wisdom in it, which is establishing the proof according to the usual habits of creation: ﴿And We certainly tested﴾, that is, "Did they reckon, while the case is that We have certainly tested," meaning: We dealt with them, by what We have of greatness, in the manner of one who tests. ﴿Those who﴾

Since the closeness in time makes the emulation (al-ta'assi) greater, He affirmed the preposition in His saying ﴿before them﴾, that is, before these to whom We have sent you, from among the followers of the prophets, to the point that a man among them would have his flesh combed with iron combs, and that would not turn him away from his religion. And among their leaders is the companion of most of the preceding surah, Musa, upon him be blessings and peace. Concerning his story there is a long report from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, called the Hadith of al-Futun (the Trials), and it is in the Musnad of Abu Ya'la. And among the last of what he was tested with (p-390) was the matter of Qarun and his followers.

Since examination is a cause for uncovering what is hidden in humans, indeed in animals, so that one is honored or humiliated in its sight, and the context guided to the meaning being: "So We will surely test them," He linked to it His saying ﴿So Allah will surely know﴾ [that is, the One who has all perfection], by testing His creation, with knowledge of witnessing (ilm shuhudi), just as He knew that by knowledge of the unseen (ilm ghaybi), and He makes it manifest to His servants even if concealment is taken to its extreme. He expressed it by the greatest Name, which indicates all the attributes of perfection, as a shift (iltifat) from the locus of greatness to something greater than it, to alert the deficient ones, who are most people, that He is free of every trace of deficiency. And He emphasized, as an indication that most people suppose steadfastness at the time of trial, and that if one conceals his deed no one will know of it, ﴿those who are truthful﴾ in their claim of faith, even if they are at the lowest levels of truthfulness. And He will surely know the truthful, who are the patient ones who say at the time of affliction ﴿This is what Allah and His Messenger promised us, and Allah and His Messenger spoke the truth﴾ [al-Ahzab: 22]. So one of them, in ease, is dutiful and grateful, and in affliction is free and patient. And He will surely know those who lied in their claim ﴿And He will surely know the liars﴾, that is, those firmly rooted in lying, who worship Allah on an edge (harf): if good befalls them they are content with it, and if a trial afflicts them they turn back upon their faces, so they lose. So each receives a recompense according to what the affliction has uncovered (p-391) of him. The use of the present tense (al-mudari') is to confirm the testing, renewing across the ages, for the two groups, the good and the wicked. So whoever does not struggle against his soul at the time of trial, obeying in ease and hardship, is among the disbelievers, and so is in Hell: ﴿Is there not in Hell an abode for the disbelievers?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 68]. And whoever strives is among the doers of good. The verse is of the ihtibak (a device in which one side is mentioned and its counterpart is left implied): by ﴿those who are truthful﴾ He indicated ﴿those who lied﴾, and by ﴿the liars﴾ He indicated ﴿the truthful﴾. He mentioned the verb first as a sign of its opposite being implied second, and the noun second as a sign of the omission of its opposite first.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 4:

When He, glorified is He, had established by this His all-encompassing knowledge and His perfect power in this world, He balanced it with what entails the like of that in the Hereafter. So the sum of what has passed of the interrogation is: "Do people think that We will not have power over them and will not know their conditions in this world? Or do they think that this will not occur in the Next, so that their wrongdoing in this world, their abandonment of God's command, and their arrogance over His servants would go in vain, and Our creating them would be pointless, without wisdom in it, rather the wisdom lies in leaving it?" This second meaning is what is meant by His saying, denouncing, "Am (am) hasiba" (Or did ... think). Or the meaning is that when He denounced people in general for supposing neglect, He knew that the people of evil deeds were more deserving of this judgment, so the denunciation against them was stronger. Thus He balanced the hamza (interrogative particle) with "am" (or) in the sense of denunciation, just as He balanced it with it in His saying: ﴿Have you taken a covenant with God?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 80], and the rest of the verse. Then He said: ﴿Am (am) hasiba﴾, meaning: he assumed an assumption that proceeds for him and persists [upon it], so it does not reveal to him his ignorance in it through a matter he reckons, so it is not confused for him in any way. ﴿Those who commit evil deeds﴾, meaning: those whom We restrained by the proofs of transmitted texts, supported by the demonstrations of reason, from them by prohibition against them. And He placed in the position of the two objects what contains a predicate and a subject, from His saying: ﴿that they outrun Us﴾, meaning: that they escape from Us in the manner of one who outstrips others, so they overpower Us, and We are not able to have power over them in this world by carrying out what We have decreed for them of good and evil at the times We appointed for it, and in the Abode of the Hereafter by reviving them after We have caused them to die, then gathering them to the place of recompense, humbled and abased, so that We recompense them for what they did and exact retribution for those they wronged among them, and the manifestation of Our adorning Ourselves with the attribute of justice regarding them becomes apparent.

When He denounced this, He marveled at those who entertain it in their breasts, magnifying the denunciation, and said: ﴿Evil is what they judge﴾, meaning: how evil is this judgment that they have passed on themselves, because the weakest of them in intellect does not accept for his servants that some of them wrong others and then he does not do justice between them; so how do they suppose of Us what they do not accept for themselves?

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 5:

When He had instilled fear in His servants, both the good-doers and the evildoers, and had lashed them all with the whip of subjugation, He alluded, by way of hinting at the threat against the liars, to the explicit enticement of the truthful (p-393). So He said, by way of inference from what preceded: ﴿Whoever hopes﴾. He expressed it thus because hope suffices as a substitute for fear of Him, glory be to Him: ﴿for the meeting of God﴾, that is, the One who unites all attributes of perfection, so it is not permissible for Him to abandon the resurrection (al-ba'th), for that would be a deficiency and a contradiction of wisdom (hikmah). He likened the resurrection to a meeting (liqa') because many veils are removed by it and the recompense becomes present.

Since those who deny the resurrection are many, He emphasized, saying in the place of "so let him beware and let him be given good news": ﴿Indeed the term of God﴾, magnifying the matter, affirming it, and making it awesome. That is, the Sovereign, the Most High, to whom belongs absolute self-sufficiency and all attributes of perfection, the appointed term for that ﴿is surely coming﴾, with no escape from it, for it is not permissible for Him that the breaking of His promise should occur. For this reason He expressed it with the Greatest Name, and to indicate that the terrors of the meeting cannot be encompassed by counting nor confined by any limit. Therefore let whoever counsels his own soul strive and struggle against it accordingly. And He, the Most High, said: ﴿And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾, that is, He alone, urging the purification of the outward and the inward, in belief, speech and action.

When he had urged them to act, he explained that action benefits none but the one who acts, so that there would not occur to the mind anything that brings the fatigue of this world and the misery of the Hereafter, namely the belief in what does not befit His majesty, exalted is He. So he said, connecting to what is implied in the structure: "Whoever gives his self rest in this world, then he only harms his own self" (p. 394). ﴿And whoever strives﴾, i.e., exerts his effort to the utmost, as if he were racing another in righteous deeds, ﴿then he strives only for himself﴾, because the benefit of that accrues to him. So he tires it in order to give it rest, afflicts it in order to make it happy, and causes it to die in order to give it life. He referred to it as "self" (nafs) because it is the one that commands to evil. He omitted the supposed implied clause because the context concerns striving. Then he gave a reason for this restriction by his saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, i.e., the One exalted above every trace of deficiency, ﴿is Free of need﴾. He emphasized it because the abundance of commands may often lead the ignorant to suppose need, and this is the wisdom in using the Greatest Name (al-ism al-a'zam, the Supreme Name). He explained that His self-sufficiency is absolute self-sufficiency by his saying, in place of "from Him," ﴿from the worlds﴾. Therefore no obedience benefits Him, and no disobedience harms Him.

The commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 7:

Since the expected construction would have been: "As for those who disbelieve and do evil deeds, We shall surely requite them all," but he omitted it because the context concerns the people of hope, he followed it with His saying: ﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾, confirming their faith, ﴿righteous deeds﴾ in hardship and ease, according to their capacity. By His saying: ﴿We shall surely expiate from them their misdeeds﴾, he indicates that a person, however diligent he is, must stumble, because he is created with a disposition toward imperfection. Thus prayer to prayer is an expiation for what lies between them, so long as major sins are not committed; and Friday to Friday, and Ramadan to Ramadan, and similar things reported in the traditions from the Prophet, the chosen one (ﷺ). And He increased it in grace and honour in His sight. Al-Baghawi said: "Takfir (expiation) is the removal of an evil deed by a good deed; or [it means]: 'We shall surely forgive them the polytheism and what they did in it.'" (p-395) And He emphasised it, because a person is disposed to retaliate against one who has wronged him, even with a word, and even by [mentioning forgiveness as a favour]; so he hardly achieves anything other than what he was formed upon. When He gave them the good news of pardon from punishment, He completed the good news with a favour [of reward], saying, linking it to what is implied: "And We shall surely establish for them their good deeds," ﴿and We shall surely recompense them﴾, that is, in Islam, ﴿the best of what they used to do﴾, that is, a state which brings them to the utmost desire, ﴿they do﴾; that is, the best reward for what they did in Islam and before it, and it is in their nature to do it.

When He, glory be to Him, mentioned that trials are inevitable, warned those who disbelieve, and gave good tidings to those who are patient, He said, linking it by conjunction to ﴿And We certainly tried﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 3], pointing to the magnification of the sanctity of the parent, since He placed it within the context of magnifying the Creator, and to the fact that it is the greatest trial: ﴿And We enjoined﴾, according to what We possess of greatness, ﴿upon man﴾, i.e., the one whom We helped to do so by making him inclined to intimacy with his kind, especially toward one who does him good, so how much more toward the one most dear to him. That is a trial for him: ﴿concerning his parents﴾.

Since the implied meaning was: "So We said to him: Act toward them ﴿with goodness﴾," i.e., an act of goodness in his kindness toward them and in his tenderness toward them, He followed this with His saying: ﴿But if they strive with you﴾, i.e., they both act with you as one who strives against someone he is striving with, and they exhaust their effort in struggling with you, ﴿to make you associate﴾ [others with Me], and He omitted the manifestation of greatness in favor of explicitly stating the intended meaning, so He said: ﴿with Me﴾. He alerted him to the need to seek proof in matters of fundamental belief, indicating the gravity of the position on account of the greatness of the matter at stake, and He said, using justice and indicating through the negation of knowledge the negation of all sciences: ﴿about which you have no knowledge﴾ (p-396) at all, that it deserves to be associated [with Him]. For whoever worships what he does not know to merit worship is a disbeliever. ﴿So do not obey them﴾, for there is no obedience to a created being, however great, in disobedience to the Creator. This requires that no one at all commit shirk, for there is certainly no doubt at all that there is no doubt that anyone other than Him, exalted is He, deserves divinity, so how much less with a proof that would necessitate knowledge? The purpose of the context of the discourse is to show fairness and to alert to sincere counsel, so that it would be more likely to be accepted. Then he gave the reason for that with His saying: ﴿To Me is your return﴾, i.e., all of you: whoever believed and whoever associated [others], by gathering on the Day of Resurrection. Then He made the following a consequence of it: ﴿And I will inform you﴾, i.e., I will tell you with a great, thorough, and eloquent report ﴿of what you used to be﴾, i.e., of your inclination, ﴿doing﴾, i.e., so stop at My limits, abandon what your desires make attractive to you, and beware of My recompense for the little and the much of that. He, glory be to Him, expressed through the cause, which is the informing [lit. because there is no ambiguity in it], the effect, which is the recompense, in an absolute expression, and as a strong threat by way of allusion, and He omitted mentioning it, because pardon may enter into it. This verse was revealed concerning Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas (may Allah be pleased with him), who embraced Islam and was dutiful toward his mother. She swore: "I will neither eat nor drink until you return from your religion, or die, so that you will be reproached for it and it will be said, 'the slayer of his mother.'" So she remained for two days and two nights. He said: "O mother, even if you had a hundred souls and they left you one soul after another, I would not abandon my religion. So eat, or if you wish, do not eat!" When she despaired of him, she ate and drank. The origin of the story is in al-Tirmidhi.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 9:

Since the implied construction is: "As for those who associate partners with God and do evil deeds, We shall certainly cause them to enter among the corrupters" — but he omitted it because the context points to it — he joined to it [as an added exhortation to kindness toward the two parents] his saying: ﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ in ease and in hardship ﴿righteous deeds﴾.

Since the righteous person is generally in a bad state in this world and has a diminished share of it, and his enemy denies most strongly that his condition should be good, He emphasized His saying: ﴿We shall certainly cause them to enter﴾, i.e., by a promise that admits no breaking, ﴿among the righteous﴾. And how excellent an entrance it is! For it is among the most eloquent descriptions of the believers.

(p. 398)

When the description of the previous categories was complete, those who hope, those who strive, and those who do righteous deeds, then, as has been indicated, among the people is one who believes in God. When he is harmed for God's sake, he endures patiently and seeks reward, awaiting recompense from the Most High, the Exalted. However, [the verse] omitted from each sentence what was indicated by what was mentioned in the other. It joins to it: ﴿And among the people﴾, that is, the wavering ones, ﴿is one who says﴾, that is, with his tongue, without tranquility in his heart: ﴿We believe in God﴾, that is, the One who is singled out for the attributes of perfection. After the allusion, it points, through the use of the plural pronoun in the attribution, to the large number of this kind, [and it indicates] that harm in this abode is an inescapable necessity that cannot be avoided. This is expressed with the particle of confirmation: ﴿So when he is harmed﴾, that is, as a trial for him and a test, by any harmer whatsoever, ﴿for God's sake﴾, that is, because of his being in the way of God, to whom nothing comparable in His greatness and all His attributes exists, through a tribulation by which He empowers His servants over him. ﴿He considers﴾, that is, that one who claimed faith, ﴿the trial of people﴾, that is, for him, by what befalls him of their harm to his body, which, when it dies, their harm to him ceases, ﴿as the punishment of God﴾, that is, the One who encompasses everything, from which escape is not hoped for. Thus the one who is tormented, after his haughtiness and arrogance, turns to submission and humiliation, because He has no equal and no protector against Him, so His punishment cannot be endured, for He has power over both the spirit and the body, and it is not possible to be separated from Him, nor from either of them, by death or by life, except by His will. Thus the action of this tormented one, when people torment him, is obedience to them in everything they command him, outwardly and inwardly. Then it becomes clear that he was lying in his claim of faith. [The verse also restricts hope to the King, the Judge of Recompense.] It indicates, through the particle of doubt, that the trial may continue until death and its duration may be long. And it emphasizes, to make every listener find it unlikely that any slander should come from anyone, in His saying: ﴿And if there comes a victory﴾, that is, for the party of God, those firm in faith.

Since the bestowal from Him is purely an act of grace, and nothing is obligatory upon Him toward anyone, (p. 399) He expressed it with words indicating that, pointing out that He does it for the sake of the Prophet (ﷺ). So He said: ﴿from your Lord﴾, that is, the One who benefits you by granting victory to the people of your religion, confirming His promise to them and bringing joy to you.

Since this state is one of ease, He used the plural pronoun, alluding to the saying of the poet:

"How many brothers there are when you count them, but in calamities they are few."

So He said: ﴿they will surely say﴾, that is, these who did not endure patiently, in deception toward the believers, out of fear and hope. He used the singular in the state of hardship, lest it be supposed that the plural is a restriction. He used the plural here to indicate that they are not ashamed of lying, even before the eyes of all witnesses. And they emphasized, because they knew that their saying would be denied, since they are liars, so they said: ﴿Indeed we were with you﴾, that is, we did not separate from you in our hearts, even though we obeyed those others with our tongues.

Since the implied sense is: Are not our allies, who discern their states, knowledgeable?, He joined to it, rebuking their saying: ﴿Is not God﴾, who encompasses the knowledge of the inward as He encompasses the knowledge of the outward, ﴿more knowing of what is in the breasts of the worlds﴾, that is, all of them, among them, so nothing of that is hidden from Him, whether it is sincerity or hypocrisy. Rather, He is more knowing than the possessors of breasts of that.

When he denied that they had knowledge, he then stated the knowledge explicitly, saying, promising and threatening, and joining it (by ʿaṭf) to what the context (al-siyāq) implies, such as: "Allah has certainly known all that they conceal and all that they disclose": ﴿And Allah will surely know﴾, that is, the One who encompasses everything in knowledge and power in the world of witnessing (ʿālam al-shahādah), until that becomes manifest to you just as He knows it in the unseen world (ʿālam al-ghayb), ﴿those who believe﴾, that is, faith has occurred from them. And He will surely know the believers, with a truthful faith [in] what He tests them with of trials (miḥan), and they do not increase except in submission and contentment. He emphasized it because of what He had mentioned earlier, that people thought they would not be tested. ﴿And He will surely know﴾ those who are hypocrites, and He will surely know the ﴿hypocrites﴾ by the same means, through the earthquakes (zalāzil) and tribulations (fitan) by which they incline with each one, however it turns them, until everyone who has understanding (lubb) knows that they have no faith, just as they have no faith. There is no doubt that He treats each of the two groups according to what it deserves, in accordance with what He knows of their hearts. This verse is of the device of ihtibāk (a rhetorical device in which one of two parallel elements is omitted and understood from the other), as has passed [at] ﴿So Allah will surely know those who are truthful, and He will surely know the liars﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 3].

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 12:

Since the context concerns persecution and harm inflicted for the sake of God, whose matter is certain, He (exalted is He) stated it with "idha" (when) rather than "in" (if). The unbelievers used to persecute those who had embraced Islam at the outset of the matter. So He (exalted is He) mentioned some of what they would say to them at the time of persecution, out of ignorance of God and delusion, and He said, expressing wonder at them (p-401), joining it by conjunction to ﴿And among the people is he who says﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 10]: ﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾, out of their presumption before God and their audacity toward His inviolable sanctuary, ﴿to those who﴾, that is, to the group who say with their tongues, "We believe in God," and who are the ones who ﴿believed﴾, that is, in truth; (the disbelievers said this) out of their ignorance of the cheerfulness of faith and the lights of recognition that had mingled with their hearts: ﴿follow﴾, that is, burden yourselves to follow ﴿our way﴾, that is, the path of our religion. They joined their promise of recompense for that to the form of a command, in conjunction with their command for them to follow, to indicate that it is certain and beyond doubt. So they said: ﴿and we will bear your sins﴾, with a true promise and a binding, decisive command, (on the premise) that if what you say is true, that there is indeed for us a return in which we will be held accountable for sins. But by my life, had they known what the news is, on the day they say, "There is no escape" (p-401), they would not have exposed themselves to this peril. On the day when every person would wish that he could ransom himself with his wealth and his sons, his spouse and his brother, his close companion and his father. Their statement, although it is in the form of a command, carries the meaning of a report, because it is a promise that God (exalted is He) has denied, since its meaning is: if sin is written against you, we will bear it on your behalf with a promise that admits no failure. ﴿And they are not﴾, that is, the disbelievers, ﴿bearers﴾ at all, outwardly or inwardly, ﴿of their sins﴾, that is, of the believers' sins, ﴿of anything﴾, though they are able not to bear them, or a burden that would lighten the punishment for them. That is: when they witness those circumstances, and their minds are overwhelmed in the seas of those terrors which mountains cannot withstand (p-402), they will disown those who said this statement to them. They reported what does not correspond to reality. It is also possible that they deliberately lied at the time of reporting, if their intention was that they would not fulfil it, on the assumption that the reward is certain.

Since their lying is known in every case, whether they deliberately intended it or not, He stated it explicitly as an affirmation of the content of what preceded it, emphasizing it for the sake of those whom they deceived, who thought them truthful in their saying, [in a resumptive construction]: ﴿Indeed they are liars﴾.

Since everyone who sets someone on a path becomes a partner in the deed done along it, he bears a like burden of its sin if it is a path of ruin, and has a like reward if it is a path of guidance. Almighty God said, emphasizing against their denial of the Hereafter and all that is in it: ﴿And they will surely bear﴾, that is, the disbelievers, ﴿their own burdens﴾, which they laid upon their weak selves through what they earned, ﴿and other burdens﴾ for others, ﴿along with their burdens﴾, through what they caused by way of leading others astray and establishing the unjust traditions that continue after them. Whoever establishes an evil tradition bears its burden and the burden of whoever acts by it until the Day of Resurrection, without this detracting in the least from the burdens of those who act by it.

Since questioning carried out in a manner of contempt and humiliation produces in the heart a dread that acts alone do not, He said: ﴿And they will surely be questioned﴾, that is, by everyone whom the Lord has commanded to question them, ﴿on the Day of Resurrection﴾, that is, the Day they used to deny and treat with contempt. The emphasis is either against their denial of that Day, or because of the presumption that one who knows is not questioned about what he knows,

﴿about what they used to fabricate﴾, that is, with the utmost eagerness, ﴿they used to invent﴾, that is, they deliberately lied about it, and they applied their minds to committing it [and persisted in it]. The use of the form of the reflexive verb (iftiʿal, "ifta'ala") indicates that they knew the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ) and deliberately lied in their promises to those whom they deceived.

Since the context concerns trial and testing, patience under humiliation, and establishing Allah's knowledge and power to save the obedient and punish the disobedient, He mentioned from among the noble Messengers, peace and blessings be upon them, one whose patience under trial was long and whose resolve in advising the servants did not weaken despite the harm they inflicted on him. This was a consolation for His Messenger (ﷺ) and his followers, may Allah be pleased with them, a strengthening of them, and a warning to Quraysh. So He said, conjoining with ﴿And We certainly tested those before them﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 3] something that serves as an explanation of it. It has a great connection to ﴿And We have certainly caused the word to reach them﴾ [al-Qasas: 51], and He emphasized it to repel the misconception of one who says that the power to control hearts makes the Messenger unnecessary in the abode of causation (tasabbub): ﴿And We certainly sent﴾, i.e., by virtue of Our greatness, which makes the Messenger unnecessary, enacting affairs according to what this abode requires of the wisdom of causation (p-404) ﴿Noah﴾, i.e., the first of Allah's messengers to the two horizons (east and west) of mankind. This is the meaning of ﴿to his people﴾, for disbelief had spread among the people of the earth. He (ﷺ) was the Prophet who suffered the longest affliction from them. For this reason, He said, as a consequence of that and as a sequel: ﴿So he remained among them﴾, i.e., after the Message, calling them to Allah. The matter is magnified by His saying ﴿a thousand﴾, so He mentioned the head of the numbers, beyond which there is no greater head. He expressed it with the word ﴿year﴾ to disparage the days of disbelief, and said ﴿less fifty﴾, thereby confirming that this period was nine hundred and fifty years, without addition or subtraction, with brevity and sweetness. He said ﴿years﴾ to indicate that the time of his life, peace be upon him, after their drowning was pleasant, broad and good, through the faith of the believers and the fertility of the land.

Since repeating the call despite non-response is more indicative of steadfastness and of not tiring, He said, as a consequence of his remaining among them and of his calling them, and as a sequel to it: ﴿So the flood seized them﴾, i.e., all of them, with drowning, a seizing of overpowering and dominance. ﴿The flood﴾, i.e., of water, because "ṭūfān" originally applies to anything that spreads, overwhelms, encompasses, prevails, and is filled abundantly, intensely and forcefully, whether a torrent, darkness, death, or other things. Here what is meant is water. ﴿While they were wrongdoers﴾, i.e., deeply immersed in this attribute, which is placing things in other than their proper places, like one who walks in the deepest darkness, through their denial of their Messenger and their persistence in their disbelief. This was constant with his calling them night and day, and of them only a few returned from error, and they are not counted due to their scarcity (p-405). He indicated this, as a consequence of that, by His saying

﴿فَأنْجَيْناهُ﴾ *So We delivered him*, that is, Noah, peace be upon him, by Our majesty, which nothing can overcome. ﴿وأصْحابَ السَّفِينَةِ﴾ *and the companions of the ship*, from among his offspring and followers, from drowning. And what is the number of the people of a single ship in count and multitude? ﴿وجَعَلْناها﴾ *and We made it*, that is, the deed or the ship, meaning itself and its kind, with that majesty, ﴿آيَةً﴾ *a sign*, that is, a token of God's power, His knowledge, His delivering of the obedient and His destruction of the disobedient, ﴿لِلْعالَمِينَ﴾ *for the worlds*. No event greater than it, stranger than it, or more famous has occurred in time, in the spreading of water over all the earth in its length and breadth, the drowning of everything upon it of living beings, both human and non-human, and the rescue of some people among them through what He had prepared before the act, a cause whose benefit endures through the repetition of long ages and the succession of times. As for it being a sign: for the human beings of that time the matter is clear. As for the other animals, they knew, from their knowledge of observed particulars, that from this water there is no escape in the abode of causes except by this ship. So the guidance to making it for salvation before the cause of destruction occurred indicates complete knowledge and comprehensive power. And whoever was guided to it, apart from all the people of that age, was guided only by God's informing him, and not otherwise. The first half of the first verse of this story is consolation and solace, serving as evidence for the two verses of trial at the beginning of the surah. Its second half is warning and caution, [and in it] evidence for the third verse, and the third verse, and the other verse is good tidings and hope, [and in it] evidence for what follows.

(p-406)

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 16:

Since the trial of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was great in being cast into the fire and in being expelled from his land, He followed it with it, saying: ﴿And Abraham﴾, meaning: ﴿And We certainly sent Abraham﴾. It is also permissible that the implied meaning be: Remember Abraham, your greatest father, so that you may take him as an example and find consolation, and so that your people may take warning from his story. But His saying "And to Madyan" favours the first reading. It indicates his prompt readiness to obey with His saying ﴿when﴾, meaning: at the time when. This is a *badal ishtimal* (substitution of inclusion, where the substituted term includes what it refers to) according to the second reading, because the times include what came before them. ﴿He said to his people﴾, those among whom he was: ﴿Worship Allah﴾, meaning: the Greatest King, by obeying what He commands you. ﴿And fear Him﴾, meaning: be wary of Him, lest you associate anything with Him, for He will punish you. ﴿That﴾, meaning: this great matter, which is your sincerity in your worship of Him and your piety, ﴿is better for you﴾, meaning: than everything. ﴿If you know﴾, meaning: [if you are] by the sound natural dispositions you possess, ﴿you know﴾, meaning: [if you are] among those who acquire knowledge (p. 407). You say that it is better, meaning: you believe this and act upon it. If you do not act upon it, then you are among the dumb animals, nay, more astray, for they are guided to what benefits them, so they turn toward it and strive with their effort to reach it.

When He had commanded them with what preceded, and negated knowledge from those who were ignorant of its goodness, He indicated it by His saying: ﴿Indeed, what you worship﴾. Since Allah is exalted above everything, He said: ﴿besides Allah﴾, meaning the One who has no likeness, no equal, [no second] and no minister. He said: ﴿idols﴾ (awthanan), pointing to the dispersal of concern through the multiplicity of what is worshipped, and multiplicity necessarily entails division, and there is no good in division. The root "w-th-n" (وثن), in all its permutations, is of the waw type, the ya' type and the hamzated type, and it revolves around increase and multiplicity, and it necessarily entails division through disagreement of word, and therefore it necessarily entails softness, and then incapacity. Its permutations are nine: three of the waw type, *wathana, thanawa, thawana*; three of the ya' type, *thana, nathā, thayana*; and three of the hamzated type, *anatha, athana, nata'a*.

From the meaning of increase comes *al-wathan* (وَثَن, idol). Al-Qazzaz said: Abu Mansur said: The difference between *al-wathan* and *al-sanam* (صَنَم, image) is that *al-wathan* is everything that has a body (جُثّة) of wood, stone, silver, gold, jewel or other material, which is carved and erected and then worshipped, while *al-sanam* is a form that has no body. Some of them made *al-wathan* and *al-sanam* the same, and this concludes his words.

And ʿAbd al-Haqq said: al-Harawi said: Ibn ʿArafa said: Whatever has a form, of plaster, stone or other than that, is a *wathan*, and this concludes his words.

From this it is known that it must have a form or a body. In any case, it is a repetition of what resembles its form or its body and an addition to it. Abu Hatim Ahmad ibn Hamdan al-Razi said in *Kitab al-Zina*: The *sanam* is a statue of stone in the form of a human being. If it is of wood, it is a *wathan*. It is also made of plaster. Sometimes they also depicted the form of a human being on a wall, and that form is also called a *wathan*. The Christians do this, and they depict in their churches the form of the Messiah and the form of Mary, and they prostrate to them. And: *istawthana al-mal* means it became fat, so its flesh increased. *Istawthana min al-mal* means he sought to increase it. *Al-nahl* (the bees) became two groups, small and large. *Al-ibil* (the camels): their young grew up with them. *Awthana Zaydan* means he gave him an abundant gift. *Al-wathin* is that which is firm, lasting in its place, so the increase in it is relative to its time. It is possible that it comes from softness, for nothing remains in this form except what has no power of movement.

And from the meaning of dispersal: *nathā al-ḥadīth* (نثا الحديث), with the nun placed first, *yanthūhu* and *yanthīhu*, of the ya' and waw types, means he spread it and related it. And *shay'a* means he scattered it and made it known. And *anthā* means he backbit and felt disgust at a thing, and one feels disgust at it only on the basis of its being spread. *Al-thuwayna* (الثُّوَيْنا), like *al-huwayna*, is a thin piece placed under the bread so that it may be levelled and evened out, so that its unevenness is removed. *Al-tathāwun* means cunning and deception, for these occur only from gathering of thought and alertness of observation, and they also occur only from one who is incapable of taking openly. From this comes *tathāwana li-l-ṣayd* when he came to it once from its right and once from its left. *Al-thanyu* of everything is that part of it which is folded over another part, and from a valley it is its bend; *ithnawā* means it bent. *Al-thinā'* (الثَّناء), like *kitāb*, is the tether of a camel, which is a doubled rope with which the camel's foreleg is tied, so that it is folded. *Al-finā'* (the courtyard) is so called because it is much frequented and repeatedly visited. *Athnā' al-shay'* means its strengths and capacities. *Al-ithnān* means twice the one; its feminine is *thintān*, and its origin is *thanā*. *Al-ithnayn* and *al-thunā*, like *ilā*, is a day of the week. *Thanaytuhu 'an wajhihi* means I turned him back from his face, so that he has a return after departure. *Thanaytu al-rajulayn* means I became the second of the two of them while you are one of them. One does not say *thannaytu fulānan*, but one says *ṣirtu lahu thāniyan*. *Al-mathānī* means the Qur'an, or a repetition of it time after time, or al-Hamd, or al-Baqara up to Bara'a (thus he expressed it in al-Qamus). In *Mukhtaṣar al-ʿAyn* it is said: a surah whose first is al-Baqara and whose last is Bara'a. In al-Qamus he mentioned other sayings on that. And among the strings of the lute [which come after] the first, its singular is *muthannā*. *Mathnā al-ayādī* means the repetition of a favour twice or more. *Al-thaniyya* means the pass, or its path, or the mountain, or the way in it, because by ascending and descending it, or by its windings, it is as if it were folded twice. *Al-thanāyā* of the teeth are the four in the front of the mouth: two above and two below. The she-camel that has entered her sixth year, the male camel *thaniyy*, the mare that has entered her fourth year, and the sheep [in its third year] are like the cow; and it seems that all of that is from a breadth that turns the animal in its fold. *Al-thaniyya* is the palm tree excepted from the bargaining. *Al-thaniyya*, *al-thanā'* is a description with praise or blame, or specifically with praise, because it is repeated. *Al-thiʿīn* with kasra is one who extracts pearls from the sea, because he repeats diving until he finds them and leaves his place for that and separates the pearls from their place. *Al-thiʿīn* also means the pearl-driller, because the hole separates its parts, and because the drill itself moves, so it increases its movement when it is done to it.

From the hamzated [root]: *na'atha 'anhu* means he went far away. *Al-munātha*, with a damma, means the one who is removed. *Al-anthīn* means the noble, because he is the second to his origin. From softness comes *al-unthā*, the opposite of the male. *Al-anīth* of iron is soft iron, which is what is not male. *Al-mu'annath* is the effeminate. *Al-unthayān* are the two testicles and the two ears. [And] *arḍ anītha* and *mi'nāth* means easy ground. *Sayf mi'nāth* is a blunt sword, that is, one that is weak and does not cut. Thus it has become clear that the whole root revolves around what does not befit the rank of divinity: multiplicity, [and] division, and softness. For this reason He came with the form of restriction, which is *qaṣr qalb* (a restriction by reversal), for the negation of what they believed concerning them of divinity.

When He indicated to them that they are not fit for that lofty rank and that exalted, sublime goal, through their multiplicity, He also indicated to them their deficiency by depicting them. So He said, in the present tense, indicating what is seen at every moment of the renewal of their coming into being: ﴿and you create﴾, that is, you shape with your hands, ﴿a falsehood﴾, that is, a thing turned away from its real face, for it is created while you call it by the name of the Creator, and it is created (*marbūb*) while you consider it a lord, and it is a servant while you make it an object of worship. Or you say concerning it that they are gods, falsely.

Since man is always in need, and he is always turned toward whoever benefits him, and since He, glorified be He, had indicated the deficiency of their objects of worship by negating good from them, He stated explicitly their incapacity and established His exclusive possession of good, so that the deserving of worship to the exclusion of them would result. He emphasized it, refuting what they supposed about their benefit and harm, and He said: ﴿Indeed those whom you worship﴾, in error and deviation from the manifest truth, ﴿besides Allah﴾, who encompasses the attributes of perfection, who is exempt from defects of imbalance, [who cannot be filled, all that is beneath His rank by anything, so how about His lofty rank and His sublime presence] ﴿they do not possess for you﴾, that is, while you worship them, how then for others, ﴿provision﴾, that is, any part of the provision without which you have no sustenance. Hence there follows His saying: ﴿so seek﴾. He indicated with the form *ifti'āl* (the seeking) the striving in it, because it is His custom, glorified be He, that in most cases He does not give it except with toil from the one provided for and effort, either in worship and trust, or in visible striving to attain it through worldly means. [And the incapable is one who follows his soul's desires and wishes for vain hopes from Allah.]

When He had indicated that, He indicated the generality in seeking, and that one should not believe that there is no escape from the means, but that the matter, along with that, is in His hand: if He wills, He grants success, and if He wills, He disappoints. He said: ﴿with Allah﴾, that is, the One who possesses every attribute of perfection, ﴿the provision﴾, that is, all of it, for there is nothing of it except that it is in His hand, and every existing thing is included in it, for everything was created for that. So His creation was perfected and some of it was bound to another, so that if anything were lacking from it the order would be disrupted, and the rulings would be voided. ﴿And worship Him﴾, that is, worship which He accepts, which is what is pure of association, for whoever is like that deserves it, rewards the worshipper of Him, and punishes the one who renounces it. So let not the pursuit of provision through apparent means distract you from His worship, for they are the true means only in appearance; a servant is often deprived of provision because of a sin he commits. ﴿And be grateful﴾, that is, perform gratitude ﴿to Him﴾ alone, for the blessings He has poured upon you. Then He gave the reason for that by His saying: ﴿to Him you will be returned﴾, that is, alone, in meaning, in this world and the Hereafter, that there is in reality no judgment for anyone other than Him, and in sensory terms, through resurrection and gathering after death, with the easiest matter, so He will reward the obedient and punish the disobedient in both abodes.

(p-414) Since the implied sense was: "If you believe, then it is your good fortune in this world and the Hereafter," he followed it with His saying: ﴿And if you deny﴾. What indicates this omitted element is this conjunctive wāw (wāw al-ʿaṭf) which joins to something that has no known antecedent. ﴿Then﴾, that is, the knowledge you have that ﴿many nations﴾ in past ages ﴿before you﴾ denied (their messengers), such as ʿĀd, Thamūd, the people of Nūḥ (Noah) and others, suffices as admonition and warning. The affair concerning them followed one uniform course that never varied: the obedient to the Messenger were saved and the disobedient to him were destroyed. That did not harm the Messenger in any way, and they harmed no one but themselves. ﴿And the Messenger is not (responsible)﴾ for compelling you to believe; rather, what is incumbent upon him is ﴿only the clear delivery﴾ (al-balāgh al-mubīn), the message that makes the matter clear, which, together with its own evident nature, leaves no room for doubt, through displaying the miracle and establishing proofs for the Oneness (of God).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 19:

Since the implied sense is: "Have you not seen their overthrown ends, and the consistency of their condition in their affair? That should suffice as a deterrent for you," he attached the following to it, to indicate a return to it, disapproving of their saying: ﴿Have they not seen﴾ with the second-person address in the reading of Hamzah and al-Kisa'i, and in a narration from Abu Bakr from 'Asim, following the preceding sequence; and with the third-person in the reading of the rest, turning away from them to signify anger ﴿how Allah originates﴾, that is, the One who possesses every perfection, ﴿the creation﴾, that is, He renews its origination at every moment. It is pronounced with a damma as "ubdi'" (from abda'a), and it has been read with a fatha as "bada'a" (from bada'a). Both, together, carry the meaning of bringing into existence from nothing. (p-415) Al-Qazzaz said: "abda'tu al-shay' ubdi'uhu ibda'an" meaning, when I brought the thing into existence, and Allah is al-Mubdi', that is, the One who originated creation. It is said: "bada'ahum" and "abda'ahum." In the Qamus: "bada'a Allah al-khalq" means He created them, like "abda'a." Their seeing of the origination is present in animals; and in plants, origination and restoration. There is no difference in restoration between one thing and another, so His saying ﴿then He restores it﴾, that is, He renews its restoration at every instant, is coordinated with ﴿originates﴾. Had it not been so, its coordination with it would be on the basis that witnessing the state of origination is made equivalent to witnessing the state of restoration, insofar as there is no difference; and then there would be no need for the strained effort of attaching it to the whole sentence from its beginning. Then he belittled their matter in relation to the greatness of His power, saying, mentioning the result of the preceding matter: ﴿Indeed, that﴾, that is, the origination and the restoration, and he emphasized it because of their denial, ﴿for Allah is easy﴾, because He is the One who combines every perfection, exalted above every trace of deficiency.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 20:

When the Mighty, the Majestic, had driven this proof home, concerning what the Friend (al-Khalil, Ibrahim) argued with his people, the opportunity was seized for guiding His Prophet Isma'il, upon both of them be prayers, peace, greetings and honour. That is because when he (peace be upon him) reasoned for the Oneness (al-wahdaniyyah), which entails the power to bring about the Resurrection (al-ma'ad), by invalidating the divinity of their worshipped objects, which entails the invalidation of everything resembling them, readiness was created for explicitly declaring the matter of the Resurrection, so he declared it. That was a great boast and a clear, weighty explanation, for establishing the proof against Quraysh and the rest of the Arabs. Thus his opportunity was seized and his depth was plunged into, as is the custom of the eloquent and the habit of the wise, eloquent speakers, because all of that was brought forth as consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) and as admonition for his people. So it was said: ﴿Say﴾ [i.e.: ] O Muhammad, to these who have bound themselves to what they have inherited of the doctrines of their fathers, without any doubt at all as to its soundness: It has been established that this is the word of God, since it has been established that you are incapable of producing its equal. Thus it is established that this proof is the speech of your father Ibrahim (peace be upon him), while you openly profess imitation of the fathers, not shying away from its disgrace. And there is no father greater for you than Ibrahim (peace be upon him). So if you imitate one who does not depart from him in worshipping what neither harms nor benefits, without any doubt at all, then imitate your greatest father in worshipping God alone, because he is your father. When he had established by means of the proofs in which there is no dispute, he said: or ﴿travel﴾, if you will not follow your father Ibrahim (peace be upon him), and reflect upon what he set forth of decisive proof and shining demonstration, ﴿in the earth﴾, if observing the conditions of your own lands does not suffice you.

Since the context was establishing the divinity, which requires the prompt emptying of the mind and turning the whole intellect toward reasoning about it, he used the conjunctive fa' that follows directly, saying: (p-417) ﴿Then look﴾, i.e., a look of contemplation (nazar i'tibar), ﴿how He originated﴾, i.e., your Lord who created you and provided for you, ﴿the creation﴾ from among the animals and plants, from the crops and trees, and other things contained in the mountains, plains and rough lands. This indicates that the first (creation) concerns what is more general than animals, so their acknowledgment of the return (al-i'adah) in it is fitting.

Since the primary aim was to explain the return, which is among the most important aims of the surah, in order to manifest what its opening mentioned of justice on the Day of Judgment, and they were deniers of it, he combined giving it importance by mentioning the Greatest Name (al-ism al-a'zam) explicitly after repeating it in this context more than once, and he concealed it in the context of origination, because they acknowledged Him in that, indicating that He is hidden in this abode and manifest in all attributes in that one. So He said: ﴿Then Allah﴾, i.e., the One who possesses all the attributes of perfection, so nothing escapes Him, the One clothed in majesty; so fear His wrath and beware of His punishment and vengeance. ﴿He brings forth the final creation﴾ after the first creation. Then He gave the reason for that by saying, emphatically, treating them as if they were deniers, since they denied the Resurrection: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, repeating His name as an alert after being blessed by mentioning it, and to indicate that He, in all His acts, and especially this one, is absolute, not restricted by any aspect nor conditioned by any matter, ﴿is All-Powerful over everything﴾, because the relation of all things to Him is one and the same.

(p-418) When this was established, it inevitably produced His statement, threatening after the clarification beyond which there is nothing but obstinacy: "He punishes" by His justice "whom He wills", i.e., among you and among others, in this world and the Hereafter, so no one, by intercession or otherwise, can shield from Him; "and has mercy" by His grace "on whom He wills", so no one can touch him with harm; "and to Him" i.e., to Him alone, "you will be turned" i.e., after your death, with the least effort.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 22:

When there remained no obstacle to His power to restore them that anyone could claim except their own resistance to it, He nullified that claim on the assumption that they made it, and said: ﴿And you cannot escape [Him] in the earth﴾, i.e., all of you, the Arabs and others, will not be able to frustrate Him in your resurrection and your punishment, ﴿wherever you turn in its surface and its depths﴾.

Since the discourse here looks most fully toward what follows the resurrection, where the states are outside what the intellect can independently grasp, and where the effect of power is most complete and perfect, most encompassing and most comprehensive, and since some spirits are in the heaven after death, He said: ﴿Nor in the heaven﴾ [i.e.,] even if it were supposed that you reached it after death through the gathering, or before it, because all of it is part of His dominion. How, then, could He be incapacitated by one who is within His dominion? It is also possible that there is a reference here to the story of Nimrod and his building of the tower by which he intended to reach the heaven, especially since the verses are flanked by the story of Abraham, peace be upon him, both before and after it.

When He had informed them that they were subject to His power, and there might remain the possibility that others would help them, He stated its negation explicitly, saying: ﴿Nor have you any protector or helper besides Allah﴾, i.e., all of you, you and others, O you who are gathered. He indicated the lowness of the rank of everyone other than Him by His saying: ﴿besides Allah﴾, i.e., the One who is greater than every great one. [And He emphasized the negation by affirming the preposition, so He said:] ﴿any protector﴾, i.e., a close relative who would shield you on account of kinship, ﴿nor any helper﴾ for any reason other than that, because He has no equal.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 23:

When the implied sense was: "Those who believe in the signs of their Lord and His meeting, these are the ones who hope for My mercy, and for them is an everlasting bliss," and he had commanded them to reason and threatened them so that they would turn back from error, leaving for men some of the impossibilities, he followed it with what he had cut off, saying, conjoining it to that implied sense: ﴿And those who disbelieve﴾, i.e., those who concealed what the lights of intellects had made manifest to them, ﴿in the signs of Allah﴾, i.e., the proofs of the Great King, the visible and audible ones, than which none is clearer, ﴿and in His meeting﴾, i.e., in the resurrection after death, which He announced and for which He established proof of His power over it by what is none clearer, ﴿those﴾, i.e., the remote, the hateful, the dull of understanding, who have been lowered from the rank of humanity, indeed from the rank of animal life altogether, ﴿have despaired﴾, i.e., their despair is established now, indeed from eternity, because they never hoped for the meeting of Allah for a single day, and none of them ever said: "My Lord, forgive me my sin on the Day of Recompense."

Since most of them were obstinate, he made clear that the speaker of this discourse, which is too exalted to be reached by mankind, is Allah, who has made His name famous in this arrangement, by turning to the mode of speaking in the first person, as an alert to the ears of the listeners, with what fills the breasts and breaks the backs, so He said: ﴿From My mercy﴾, i.e., from My doing to them, by way of honour, the entry into Paradise and other things, the act of the merciful; and He repeated the indication to magnify the matter, so He said: ﴿And those﴾, i.e., those for whom after their remoteness there is no remoteness; and He mocked them in the expression with the preposition of possession (lam al-milk), whose usage is predominantly for what is loved, so He said: ﴿for them is a painful punishment﴾, i.e., one that is painful, whose pain is extreme in this world and the next.

When God, glory be to Him, concluded this parenthetical sentence with what He had begun it with, and with what He had concluded the preceding words of the Friend (al-Khalil, Abraham) peace be upon him with, and this added to what you see of severe threat, He proceeded to complete his story, peace be upon him, indicating that no one can overpower Him or can help anyone against His painful punishment. He indicated that they answered his words with the opposite of what they required, as a declaration of obstinacy and persistence in corrupt belief. So He said: ﴿So the answer of his people was not but that they said﴾, that is, those from whom acceptance of his counsel was hoped, (p-٤٢١) since they knew his great compassion and the magnitude of his trustworthiness and sincere advice, ﴿with the utmost brutality﴾, ﴿"Kill him"﴾, that is, with the sword, ﴿"or burn him"﴾, that is, with fire.

When the opinion of all of them settled on this second option, and he had no supporter among them, God, glory be to Him, indicated it by His words, linking it to what is implied [as follows: The one who was held in honour refused killing, because it is a punishment customary for those among the criminals who deserve it, and he had done a unique deed in the age, so it was fitting that the punishment for it be specific, with a punishment not known the like of, which is burning, in a strange form. So they turned back from killing, and their opinion settled on burning]. So they gathered wood until it filled what lay between the mountains, lit the fire in it until it burned whatever came near it with great blazing, and hurled him into it by catapult. ﴿But God delivered him from the fire﴾ by His perfect majesty, a deliverance that was easy and immediate, without need of gradualness, ﴿from the fire﴾, that is, from its burning and its harm, and it benefited him by burning his bonds.

When his story in this context contained clear proofs and miraculous matters, God, glory be to Him, magnified its matter by His words, emphasizing it for greater alerting to its mention, and treating their hesitation regarding what the manifest signs call to, namely faith, as the position of one who denies them: ﴿Indeed in that﴾, that is, what He mentioned of his affair and what his story was adorned with of wisdoms, ﴿are signs﴾, that is, decisive proofs in indicating the whole of God's command, from His disposal over bodies and meanings, since the fire did not burn him, and it burned his bonds and every (p-٤٢٢) bird that passed over it. Despite seeing this, they did not believe, and they were unable to harm him with anything other than that.

Since the true value of a thing is in reality what benefits it, and He, glory be to Him, had veiled it by desires and preoccupying appetites from using the light of reason, He said: ﴿for a people who believe﴾, that is, who turn to using the light of reason which God bestowed upon them, so they affirm the unseen, until faith becomes, through their abundant polishing of the mirrors of their hearts by reflecting on its causes, a disposition for them such that at every moment they renew their ascent through its ranks and their movement through its tents and encampments.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 25:

Since the previous verses established that these idols have no power to benefit, he now points to a harm that follows from them, a harm so great that it has no comparison to any benefit they might offer, so that at that point it is no benefit at all. Thus Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And he said﴾, that is, Ibrahim, upon him be peace, not fearing their threats of killing or anything else, emphasizing, because of what he alluded to of their denial of the weakness and helplessness of their associates: ﴿Indeed, you have taken﴾, that is, you have adopted with contrivance and artifice, and he points to the greatness of the Creator and the exaltedness of His station by His saying: ﴿besides Allah﴾, that is, the One before whose power every thing is subdued, and there is no burden, in the belief that He is Lord, of needing a preliminary act of making or craftsmanship or anything else. He said: ﴿idols﴾, indicating their multiplicity, which is incompatible with the rank of divinity. He points to that benefit by His saying: ﴿out of affection﴾, that is, for the sake of affection among you. For those who put it in the accusative, whether they omit the tanwin, namely Hamzah and Hafs from ʿAsim and Rawh from Yaʿqub, or they apply tanwin, who are the rest [of the readers], ﴿among you﴾. For the one who put it in the genitive by way of extension (al-ittisa') and raised "affection" (mawaddah), who are Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, al-Kisa'i and Ruways from Yaʿqub, the meaning is: it is the affection of the bond uniting you, in the sense of your affection, in a more emphatic manner, because if affection exists for a bond that gathers people, it exists for those people all the more so. For the one who put it in the genitive and in the accusative, who are Hamzah and Hafs from ʿAsim and Rawh from Yaʿqub, the meaning is: for the sake of affection. For the one who put it in the accusative and applied tanwin, who are Nafi', Ibn ʿAmir, Abu Jaʿfar and Shuʿbah, "bayn" (among) is, in his view, an adverbial complement. ﴿In the life of this world﴾, through gathering around them and mutual support in their matter, just as people agree upon a school of thought and that becomes the cause of their mutual friendship. This indicates that the gathering of wickedness among the people of this world is the constant custom, and that love for the sake of Allah and gathering for His sake is exceedingly rare, because it severs the ties of this world and its desires, which have been made attractive to people, with what they contain of deception and grave peril.

When he pointed to this benefit, which is in reality a harm, he mentioned what follows from it of severe harm, saying, using the particle of distance to indicate the greatness of that day and that He had granted them in this life a term in which they could strive to protect themselves from the evil of that day: ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection﴾, he presented it as something beyond dispute, due to the proofs established for it. ﴿Some of you will disavow others﴾, so each of them will deny the good qualities of his companion and disown him, with the followers cursing the leaders and the leaders cursing the followers. And you will all deny the worship of idols at one time when you realize that they have neither harm nor benefit, and at another time you will affirm them, seeking their support and hoping for their benefit, while the idols will deny your worship and reject your benefit. ﴿And some of you will curse others﴾ regarding what was mentioned. ﴿And your refuge﴾, all of you together, you and the idols, ﴿is the Fire﴾, so that it increases your punishment and your hatred of them increases. ﴿And you will have﴾ and he intensified the negation, saying: ﴿no helpers﴾ at all, who would protect you from it. This includes everyone who agrees with his companions among the people of sin or idleness in vices, so that they consider him good in company, refined in character, and gentle in disposition, or out of fear that they would describe him with coarseness of nature and bad companionship. By my life, this has spread among the people of this age, so that they may be described as having companions of brotherhood and friendship with intimates, turning away from the pleasure of the Sovereign, the Judge.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 26:

When the context was that of trial, and he mentioned among the prophets those whose trial was long, (p-425) he made clear that there was not for them, from among their peoples, any follower able to help them, and that Allah, glory be to Him, took upon Himself their sufficiency, so that no one was able to destroy them, and He destroyed their enemies. Thus they had no helpers. So He said: ﴿So Lut believed in him﴾, meaning: because of his supplication for him, together with what he saw of the signs, ﴿Lut﴾, meaning: the son of his brother Haran, and he alone, and he was the first of the men to believe him. ﴿And he said﴾, meaning: Ibrahim, upon both of them be prayers and peace, emphasizing what was deserving of denial, namely the emigration, because of its difficulty: ﴿Indeed, I am emigrating﴾, meaning: I am leaving my land and my kinsfolk, in the manner of forsaking them, and so I am relocating and withdrawing ﴿to my Lord﴾, meaning: to a land in which there is no companion nor kinsman, nor one from whom help is hoped for, nor one whose affection is beneficial. Then satisfaction with Allah alone becomes manifest, and reliance upon Him alone, to the exclusion of all else. So he emigrated from Kuthā, in the countryside of Kufa, to Harran, and then from there to the Holy Land. Thus he had two emigrations, and he was the first to emigrate for the sake of Allah. Muqatil said: he was at that time seventy-five years old. Then he gave the reason for that, by which he consoles himself for separation from his land and the people of his affection, from his close kin, his relatives and those near to him, so he said, emphasizing, to calm whoever might follow him and to ease for him the separation from what souls have grown accustomed to, that there is no honor except through Him, from tribes, wealth and acquaintances: (p-426) ﴿Indeed, He is the Mighty﴾, meaning: He alone, so He is worthy of granting honor to whoever turns to Him, ﴿the Wise﴾, so that when He honors someone, His wisdom prevents anyone from attacking him with humiliation, by deed or word, as those did to me when they wanted to humiliate me, though I was deserving of honor from my kinsfolk and the people of my nearness, and they went to great lengths in harming me, though they were the ones deserving of benefiting me from among my own relatives and those dear to me.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 27:

Since the implied sense is: "We strengthened him by a strengthening that he had hoped for from Us, and We firmly established him so that it continued among his descendants until the Resurrection," He follows it with His saying: ﴿And We bestowed upon him﴾, that is, by the magnificence of Our power, as thanks for his migration, ﴿Isaac﴾ from his wife Sarah, peace be upon her, who combined in her youth barrenness with, in her old age, despair. The conjunction of his gift to him with the particle "wa" (and) is an indication of what will come, God willing, in Surat al-Saffat, that the one sacrificed was Ishmael, peace be upon him, because the gift there is followed by the particle "fa" (then) after the migration. ﴿And Jacob﴾, from his son Isaac, peace be upon them both.

Since the context of this surah concerns trial, and Abraham, peace be upon him, had been tested with Ishmael, peace be upon him, by separating him from his mother, may God be pleased with them both, and placing them in a barren stretch of land with no one to keep them company, He did not mention him explicitly in the context of favour. He singled out Isaac, peace be upon him, because he was not tested in him with anything of that kind, and because the favour concerning him, since his mother was aged and barren, is greater and more magnificent, for it is more wondrous. He mentioned Ishmael, peace be upon him, allusively in His saying: ﴿And We placed﴾, that is, by Our might and wisdom, ﴿in his offspring﴾, from the sons of Isaac and Ishmael, peace be upon them both, ﴿prophethood﴾, so that there was no prophet after him who was alien to him. And once this connection is established, it necessarily follows with certainty that the one sacrificed was Ishmael, peace be upon him, for this surah is devoid of mention of him. It is as if it were said: "We gave him good news of what would gladden him, [namely] Isaac, after We had commanded him with what would grieve him, [namely] Ishmael, peace be upon them both. So he was patient in the affliction of hardship, and thankful in the affliction of ease."

﴿And the Scripture﴾. No scripture was sent down except among his descendants. The singular form is used so as to indicate, together with its generic inclusion of the four Books, that nothing deserves to be written except what was revealed in them or was referring back to them. Had it been put in the plural, this meaning would not have been conveyed. ﴿And We gave him his reward﴾ for his migration ﴿in this world﴾, by what We specially granted him, of which none other than Us is capable: abundance of provision, pleasant living, many servants, children in old age, abundant offspring, good praise, and love from all of creation, and other than that.

Since the disbelieving one, in denying the Resurrection, believes that he has embittered his life by the migration with a bitterness for which there is no remedy, the situation requires emphasis in His saying: ﴿And indeed he is in the Hereafter﴾, that is, the abode and place of settlement, ﴿among the righteous﴾, those whom We have singled out with felicity and for whom We have made the best reward and an increase.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 28:

Since the context, as has passed, is that of trial (ibtila'), he gave extended narration (al-bast fi al-qass) to the one who had no supporter among his people, or who was a stranger among them (p-428). For this reason he followed the Friend (al-Khalil), upon him be prayers and peace, with his nephew, whom Allah sent to the people of Sodom: people with whom he had no kinship or clan. So He said: ﴿And Lut﴾, i.e., We sent him. He indicated his promptness in complying with the command by His saying: ﴿when﴾, i.e., and We sent him when ﴿he said to his people﴾, the people of Sodom among whom he had settled, with whom he had intermarried and to whom he had attached himself, so that they became his people, after he had parted from his uncle Abraham the Friend, upon both of them be prayers and peace, disapproving of what he saw of their condition and their abominable deeds, emphasizing it for him as a sign that he, despite their regarding him as among the most well-known of the known, was worthy of denouncing it: ﴿Indeed, you commit an abomination﴾ [i.e.,] an excess beyond bounds in ugliness, so that it is as though, for that reason, there is no abomination other than it. Then he gave the reason for its being an abomination, as a new statement, with His saying: ﴿that no one has preceded you in it﴾.
