Or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) clarifying the magnitude of their audacity toward the reprehensible, i.e., not preceded ﴿in it﴾. He made the negation more emphatic with His saying: ﴿from anyone﴾, and added with His saying: ﴿from among the worlds﴾, i.e., all of them, let alone the particular people.

Then he repeated the denunciation for emphasis, because of the extreme ugliness of what they commit, which they themselves reject. So he said: ﴿Indeed, do you approach males﴾ with lust, and he joined to it the other evils they added to it, making clear that they deserve blame in several respects. Their condition led to the assumption that they had reached such a degree of corruption that there was no hope of their turning back from it, given their persistence in it and their insistence on it without weariness or distress. So he said: ﴿and you cut off the road﴾, that is, by harming the travelling merchants and passers-by.

When he singled out these two corruptions, he then spoke generally, indicating open defiance, and said: ﴿and you commit in your nādī (assembly place, the gathering place where people sit to converse) the abomination﴾. That is, the place where you sit to talk, such that some of you can hear the calls of others from the gathering of companionship. It is called a nādī only while the people are in it; when they rise from it, it is no longer called that. ﴿The abomination﴾, that is, this kind of thing, which the sacred laws, the standards of decency and sound reason all reject, and about which you show no restraint in a society where a person restrains himself even from doing what is merely less preferable, and without any of you being ashamed before another. He indicated their obstinacy by saying, as a consequence of these admonitions against those scandals: ﴿So the answer of his people was not but that they said﴾, that is, the people among whom there was strength and courage, such that his harm and injury were to be feared and guarded against, when he denounced what he denounced to them, ﴿except that they said﴾ out of obstinacy, ignorance and mockery: ﴿Bring us the punishment of Allah﴾. They used the greatest Name in expressing greater audacity. Since the denunciation implied a threat of some harmful matter, they said: ﴿if you are﴾, that is, as one established in the state of ﴿being among the truthful﴾, that is, in your threat and your mission, goading and provoking him.

Since it was as if it were said: "With what did he answer them?", it is said: ﴿He said﴾, that is, Lut, peace be upon him, turning away from them and turning wholeheartedly toward the One who had shown him kindness: ﴿My Lord﴾

Since it was as if it were said: "With what did he answer them?", it is said: ﴿He said﴾, that is, Lut, peace be upon him, turning away from them and turning wholeheartedly toward the One who had shown him kindness: ﴿My Lord﴾

Since it was as if it were said: "With what did he answer them?", it is said: ﴿He said﴾, that is, Lut, peace be upon him, turning away from them and turning wholeheartedly toward the One who had shown him kindness: ﴿My Lord﴾

(p-432) When nothing remained after this except the account of the Messengers with Lut, peace be upon him, [al-Biqa'i] said, conjoining it to what its sense implies: "Then they departed from him and went to the city in which Lut, peace be upon him, was." By changing from the fa' (then, immediately) to the waw (and), he conveys that there is a distance between the two places: ﴿And when﴾. He retained [a form that resembles] the verbal particle (the particle "an") in accordance with what the purpose of the surah requires, and most of its contexts concern consolation in the station of trial and striving in forbidding evil. [Therefore he mentions here, in the story of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, the killing and the burning, and his good tidings were followed by the destruction of the wrongdoing town.] So He said: ﴿when Our messengers came﴾, i.e., those honoured by Us, ﴿to Lut﴾, as an explanation, because he ﴿was distressed﴾, i.e., distress came upon him, ﴿on their account﴾ at the very first moments of their coming to him and at the time of their arrival upon him. Distress overtook him without any doubt when he saw how handsome their appearance was, and he feared for them from the exposure of his people to them, while he thought they were among mankind. This is because [the "an" (that)] in such a construction is a conjunctive particle [even though its origin is the verbal noun], to affirm that the two actions occurred in sequence, one following the other, in two adjacent times with no interval between them (p-433) [for both occurred] in a single portion of time. [Ibn Hisham said in al-Mughni, in substance, that the reason for this is that the superfluous particle emphasizes the meaning of what it accompanies for its emphasis, while "lamma" restricts the occurrence of the second action to immediately after the first and makes it consequent upon it, so the superfluous particle emphasizes that.]

﴿And he was straitened on their account﴾, i.e., he was unable to devise a means of defending them, ﴿in his ability (dhar'an)﴾, i.e., the measure of his capacity, as has been explained and elaborated in the surah of Hud, peace be upon him. The origin of this expression is that whoever's arm is long attains what its short-armed counterpart cannot reach, so it became a proverb for helplessness and power. That was because they came to him in the form of very handsome youths, and he knew the affair of the people of the town concerning such [matters], yet he did not know that they were the messengers of God.

Since the intended sense was: "They said to him, 'O Lut! We are the messengers of your Lord, so relieve yourself of this constriction which we see in you, for we have only been sent to destroy them,'" he followed this with His words: ﴿And they said﴾, i.e., when they saw what he suffered over their affair: ﴿Do not fear﴾ [i.e.] that they will reach us, [or] that you or any of those who obey you will perish, ﴿and do not grieve﴾, i.e., over any of those We are destroying, for there is no good in any of them over which one should grieve on their account. Then they gave the reason for this, stressing it emphatically so as to dispense with lengthy sentences, indicating that the time is pressing and so does not admit of prolongation: ﴿Indeed, We will deliver you﴾, i.e., We are emphatic in delivering you, ﴿and your family﴾, i.e., and We will destroy the people of [this] town, so that your mind does not suppose that they will reach us. (p-434) They said: ﴿except your wife﴾, specifying each individual among them other than her. Then they indicated her destruction by their words, as an answer to one who seems to have asked: "What about her?" It was said: ﴿She was among those who remain behind﴾, i.e., as if this judgment was in the original constitution of her creation.

When the expression had made their destruction clear, as has passed, they stated it outright, specifying its kind, giving the reason for what they had reported, and emphasizing it to inform them that the matter had been decided with certainty, so that they would not intercede for them. This follows the custom of the prophets in compassion for their nations: ﴿Indeed, We will surely send down﴾, i.e., without doubt, ﴿upon the people of this town a punishment﴾, i.e., a torment in which there is violent agitation, so that whoever is struck by it is shaken, whoever he may be, ﴿from the sky﴾, so its impact is great and its blow severe, ﴿because of what they used to﴾, i.e., a firmly rooted state of being, ﴿defiantly disobey﴾, i.e., they go out at every moment from the circle of reason and modesty.

[p. 435] Since the implied sense is: "So Our messengers did what they had been commanded regarding him, delivering him and destroying all their towns, and We left it as though no one had ever dwelt there at all," He followed this with His words, emphatically, to indicate the excellence of those addressed by this story, both Arabs and others, and that between them and guidance there is nothing but reflection on their own situation together with stripping themselves of desire. ﴿And We have certainly left of it﴾, by Our own majesty, ﴿a sign﴾, meaning of that town, ﴿clear﴾, a proof of Our power over everything We will. It is the black, foul-smelling water that covered all their towns after they were sunk into the earth. It is unlike all the waters of the earth, because it is the water of wrath upon those who, by their deeds, departed from creation, and it is well known to be a consequence of the sinking.

Since the Exalted had veiled many people from perceiving with their eyes, He said: ﴿for a people who understand﴾. Thus He counted as non-understanding, and as not perceiving that it is a sign, anyone who does not gain insight from it, and as lacking the capacity to carry out what He intends.

When the context was to establish the Day of Religion (yawm al-din) and the destruction of the corrupters, and for one whose trial had lasted long among the righteous and who found no helper from his people, either because of his strangeness among them or because his kin were few and he had no followers, and Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, was among those whom his people deemed weak and whose kin they considered insignificant, since they called them a *rahṭ* (a small group), and the *rahṭ* is what is fewer than ten, or from seven to ten, while what is fewer than seven down to three is a *nafar* (a small band), so he, peace be upon him, was in this count of that sort, he followed the story of Lot with his story, peace be upon him, [so He said:] ﴿And to﴾, meaning: And indeed We sent to (p-436) ﴿Madyan their brother﴾, meaning: in lineage and in homeland, ﴿Shu'ayb﴾.

[Since the principal aim of the surah is commanding good and forbidding evil without interruption, He expressed it with *fa* and said]: ﴿So he said﴾, meaning: as a consequence of his being sent, and immediately following it, he said: ﴿O my people, worship Allah﴾, meaning: the Supreme King alone, and do not associate anything with Him, for worship in which there is association is nothing, because Allah the Exalted is above partners, so He accepts only what is purely for Him.

Since the context was to establish proofs of the resurrection, which is one of the aims of the surah, he said: ﴿And hope for the Last Day﴾, meaning: a good reward on it, so that you do what befits that, ﴿and do not commit abuse on the earth﴾ while you are ﴿corrupters﴾, meaning: deliberately intending corruption.

So too the passage: "And when this counsel was followed by their denial, and the denial was followed by their destruction—confirming that the people of evil deeds do not escape—He said: ﴿But they denied him, so the quake seized them﴾, that is, for that reason, a seizing of subjugation and overpowering, ﴿the quake﴾, that is, the blast which shook them and destroyed them. ﴿So they were in their abode﴾, that is, their dwelling-places which had been circling around them, and in which they used to move about, ﴿lying prostrate﴾, that is, fallen upon their chests, remaining in one place, unable to make any movement at all, because they had no spirits left."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 38:

Among the great aims is to show that some of these nations follow one another in good and evil in an orderly sequence, and that the destruction of those who denied and the deliverance of those who affirmed proceed generation after generation. The destruction of 'Ad and Thamud was extremely remarkable, given their renown for the strength of their bodies and the firmness of their structures. The meaning of the conclusion of the story of Madyan was "So We destroyed them," and upon that meaning He joined His saying ﴿and 'Ad and Thamud﴾, that is, We also destroyed 'Ad and ﴿Thamud﴾, despite their insolence, arrogance and haughtiness. ﴿And it has become clear to you﴾, that is, it became entirely evident in itself, O Arabs, ﴿from their dwellings﴾, that is, what has been described of their destruction and of their state of physical might, breadth of intellect, lofty concerns, keen minds and great station, when you pass by those dwellings and look at them during your travels for trade to Syria. They turned their thoughts toward enjoying the passing goods of this world, so they hoped for far-off things and built strongly, yet none of that availed them anything against the command of God. ﴿And Satan made attractive to them﴾, with the utmost embellishment, ﴿Satan﴾, that is, the one far from mercy, burned by the curse, through the strength of his deception and the beloved misguidance and trickery he had; ﴿their deeds﴾, that is, the corrupt ones. So they turned wholly toward them, along with the clear enemy, and turned away from the guiding and sincere advisers.

Since this embellishment resulted in their being barred, due to their blindness, from the straight path, He said: ﴿so he barred them from the way﴾, that is, he prevented them from traversing the road, which is the only road, because it leads to salvation, while any other leads to destruction, [p. 438] so it is non-existence, and non-existence is better than it. Since this might be thought to be due to the extreme dullness of their minds, He said: ﴿and they were﴾, that is, Satan did to them what he did of misguidance, while they were in a state of the utmost firmness, ﴿discerning﴾, that is, reckoned among people as extremely perceptive and intelligent, because of what they surpassed others in, of what they knew of the outward aspects of the worldly life, and they did not precede us [in this], but rather We brought them down through their evil deeds in what We willed of various kinds of destruction. So beware of the like of their fates, for you do not resemble them in strength, nor do you approach them in intellect.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 39:

Since the arrogance of Pharaoh and those mentioned with him was beyond concealment, given the strength they possessed in wealth and manpower, He said: ﴿And Qarun﴾, meaning: We destroyed him and his people. His falling into the causes of destruction is more remarkable, because he was from the Children of Israel, and because he was tested with wealth and knowledge. That became [the cause of his self-admiration, so he became arrogant towards Musa and Harun, peace be upon them both, and that became] the cause of his destruction. ﴿And Pharaoh and Haman﴾, his minister, who kindled the fire for him upon the clay. Neither was he saved, nor was he a leader in disbelief; rather, he sold his happiness by becoming a sin for others.

Since their destruction in the presence of the signs was more remarkable, and therefore deserving of denunciation, as an indication that witnessing the signs is worthy of being followed by faith, He said: (p-439) ﴿And Musa had certainly come to them with clear proofs﴾, meaning: proofs that left no room for doubt. So they caused, by what insight required, arrogance: ﴿But they were arrogant﴾, meaning: they sought to be greater than every great one, by their actions being the actions of those who seek that. ﴿In the land﴾, after the coming of Musa, peace be upon him, to them, [more] than they had been before him.

Since whoever is arrogant, while knowing that he will be seized, is more blameworthy than one who is ignorant of that, He said: ﴿But they were not ones who could escape﴾, meaning: those mentioned, all of them, were not, in any way, ones who could outrun what We intend for them, by slipping out of Our grip; rather, they were in Our grip, as we mentioned at the beginning of the surah, and they knew that.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 40:**

﴿So each﴾ means: as a consequence of their denial and disobedience, each of them ﴿We seized﴾, that is, by what We possess of greatness, ﴿for his sin﴾, seizing him as a punishment, so that it would be known that no one can overpower Us. ﴿Among them is one upon whom We sent﴾, sending a punishment, how great a punishment it was! ﴿a violent wind﴾, that is, a wind that hurls with the force of its blast and the severity of its crash, pelting with stones, as with 'Ad and the people of Lut. ﴿And among them is one whom seized﴾, seizing him for destruction, wrath and punishment, [and He departed from the style of greatness so that the attribution in this case would not give the impression of a voice that leads into the calamity of anthropomorphism] ﴿the Shout﴾, whose severity makes the wind that carries it, and that agrees with its purpose, manifest, so that the earth quakes at its greatness, as with Madyan and Thamud. ﴿And among them is one whom﴾ [He returned to the style of greatness used earlier, for its safety from the misconception mentioned regarding the Shout, and to draw attention to the fact that none but Allah, glorified is He, is able to do it, so that in it there is an indication of His greatness that description falls short of, and so He said:] ﴿We caused the earth to swallow him﴾, by making him disappear into it, as with Qarun and his company. ﴿And among them is one whom We drowned﴾ by immersion in water, as with the people of Nuh, Pharaoh and his armies, and the punishment of the people of Lut and Salih. These are fit for enumeration under drowning and enumeration under swallowing by the earth. Thus, at times We destroy by a wind that hurls stones from the sky, as with the people of Lut, or from the earth, as with 'Ad; at other times by a wind that strikes hearts with a cry, shaking hearts and lands; and at other times We annihilate by plunging into the dense, and at still other times by drowning in the subtle. How excellent is the insight of those who contemplate these binding decrees and reflect on these past judgments, so that they may know the reality of His saying: ﴿You cannot escape Him in the earth or in the heaven﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 22] - [the verse].

Since that might lead the obstinate to some of what they were accustomed to in their stubbornness, He said: ﴿And Allah was not﴾, that is, the One to whom belongs no majesty or perfection except Him, and for whom it is ﴿to wrong them﴾, that is, intending to deal with them as a wrongdoer deals with one who punishes one who has no crime, or one who has committed a crime but was not forewarned against his crime so that he might desist and be safe, or who persists and is destroyed. This is because no benefit reaches Him, glorified is He, from their destruction, and no harm befalls Him, exalted is His majesty, from their survival. ﴿But they were﴾, that is, [they] and no others, ﴿wronging themselves﴾ and no one else, ﴿by committing what We had informed them more than once displeases Us and that We seize whoever does it. So they did not accept counsel despite their weakness, nor did they fear punishment despite their frailty. As for what they worshipped and hoped and aspired would help them, it was even weaker than they were.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 41:

Because none of them (the idols) can avail anyone among them anything, the Sunnah (way) of God has not been disrupted concerning His friends and His enemies in any generation of generations [or any age of ages]. Rather, it has run in the most upright order and the most perfect arrangement. By this (the Sunnah's consistency) he connected His words, exalted is He, in the manner of istinsaj (close continuation): ﴿The likeness of those who﴾.

Since calling upon other than God contradicts sound reason (qawim al-'aql), clear transmitted text (sarih al-naql), and the sound natural disposition (salim al-fitrah) [and correct thought (sahih al-fikrah)], this would require [training toward] coarseness (al-jalafah) and habituation to dullness (al-kathafah). He said: ﴿have taken﴾, meaning: they relied upon taking (ittakhadhu, from ittakala, "to rely," plus an, "that they took").

Since the ranks below His rank, exalted is He, cannot be counted, and all ranks are beneath His rank, He said [alerting to this by the prepositional phrase]: ﴿besides God﴾, meaning: the One who has no equal. They were content with the lesser, in place of the One whom illusions and conjectures cannot suffice. ﴿Protectors﴾ (awliya') who, by their claim, help them, from among objects of worship and others, in weakness and frailty. ﴿Like the likeness of the spider﴾, the well-known creature with many long legs. Then he resumed mentioning the aspect of the resemblance and referred to it with the feminine, although it may be spoken of in the masculine, to magnify its weakness, because the context concerns the weakness of what it builds. He said: ﴿has taken a house﴾, meaning: it exerted itself in taking it in its making for itself, so that it may protect it from destruction and shield it from calamity, just as these people exerted themselves in fashioning their lords so that they might benefit them and, by their claim, preserve and elevate them. That house, despite its exertion in its matter and its great toil in its affair, is in the utmost frailty.

Since its state in its making is the state of one who denies its frailty, he said, emphasizing: ﴿and indeed﴾ [the wa' of it is for the circumstantial state from the pronoun in ﴿has taken﴾], meaning: while the state is that it is the frailest. This was the original form, but he made it apparent for generality and said: ﴿the frailest of houses﴾, meaning: the weakest of them, ﴿is the house of the spider﴾, which it toiled greatly in weaving and endured much in its spinning, because it gives no shelter from heat, protects not from cold, and fortifies not against a seeker. Likewise is what these have taken of these idols and this religion that has no root: it is the frailest and most flimsy of religions. ﴿If only they knew﴾, meaning: if they had any kind of knowledge, they would have benefited from it and known that this is their likeness, and so they would have kept far from believing in that whose likeness is this.

When their benefit from their knowledge was negated, the negation was valid, and they and it (the spider's house) were on an equal footing, with neither party possessing anything of what it intended. How wretched a losing bargain, and a stagnant, ruined trade!

Since striking a parable for something is valid only from one who knows that thing, and since one who supports something cannot set out to oppose it unless he knows it and knows the measure of his power and the number of his soldiers, this connects to the point that this is His (glory be to Him) condition, and that their associates are far from it. How then do they hang their hopes on their help?

This added to that beauty: its following upon the negation of knowledge from them. So He said, indicating their ignorance in their denial that anyone could destroy their gods, which are the weakest of things:

﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, meaning the One who has the attributes of perfection, ﴿knows﴾ by means of those attributes ﴿what﴾, meaning those ﴿they call upon﴾, meaning those to whom He struck the parable, or "you" in the reading with the second-person (*ta'*, al-fawqaniyyah), a shift to the mode of address (*iltifat*) signalling anger, ﴿besides Him﴾, indicating the lowliness of their rank. He emphasized the generality with His saying ﴿of any thing﴾, meaning whether it is a star, an idol, an angel, a jinn, or anything else. They do not know it, nor do they know anything of what they reach toward, so how can they intercede with Him or be helped against Him? (p-٤٤٤) To this points His saying: ﴿And He is the Mighty﴾, meaning beyond His associates knowing Him or encompassing anyone in knowledge, or anything He wills being prevented from Him. They allowed that *ma* be a negation, meaning: no thing that is counted.

Since that may have suggested that He does not know at all, He said ﴿the Wise﴾, meaning the one whose knowledge is perfect, placing everything He wills in its most perfect place. So He concealed His essence through His greatness and majesty until there is no inner reality besides Him, and manifested it through His acts and what was unveiled of His beauty until there is truly no outer reality other than Him. He overpowers whom He wills by His might, and gives respite to whom He wills by His wisdom. So let no one be deceived by His respite, supposing that it is neglect.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 43:

When He had finished with their parable, and with what its soundness depends upon, it was as if it were said, in a manner of magnifying this parable: "This is their parable." So He followed it with His saying, as an indication toward all the parables of the Qur'an, magnifying them and alerting to their lofty worth and exalted station: ﴿And these are the parables﴾, that is, those that are too lofty to be attained by any kind of stratagem. Then He resumed with His saying: ﴿We set them forth﴾ by what We possess of greatness, as a clarification ﴿for the people﴾, depicting intelligible meanings in the forms of sensible things, so that they may come close to their intellects and they may benefit from them. Such is the case with all comparisons: they are paths for understanding toward meanings that are veiled behind curtains, bringing them out, uncovering them, and rendering them in images.

Since they used to mock the parables they saw, in which mention is made of the fly, the gnat and the like, He spoke to them in a general way: ﴿And none understand them﴾, that is, none understand them as they truly should be understood, so that they benefit from them, ﴿except the knowledgeable﴾, that is, those who have been prepared for knowledge and for whom it has been made a disposition, by what He has scattered into their hearts of His lights, and what has shone in their breasts of His secrets. They place things in their proper places. Al-Harith ibn Abi Usamah narrated from Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The knowledgeable one is the one who understands from Allah and so acts in obedience to Him and avoids His displeasure." Al-Baghawi said: a mathal (parable) is a widely circulating saying that includes the likening of one thing to another.

When he had established that He, glory be to Him, cannot be frustrated and that no one can help those whom He seizes, and confirmed this by observation of the past generations that were destroyed, and brought it close to minds through the parable that reaches the highest degree of clarity, and concluded that He had veiled understanding of it from most of His creation, he indicated all of that by His saying, manifesting His power and the rest of His attributes of perfection, after having established that their protectors are in the lowest of ranks of weakness: ﴿God created the heavens and the earth with truth﴾, meaning: He to whom none can be compared in greatness, majesty, beauty, or perfection. ﴿With truth﴾ means: a matter to which reality conforms; or by means of showing that reality conforms to His report; or by means of establishing the truth and nullifying falsehood. So you will not find anyone who understands Him (p-446) with a true understanding, despite their equality in humanity, except that he is one of the people of tranquility, humility, and peace, and no one who seeks to seize him can frustrate Him, and no one who disobeys His prophets prospers. Thus His might became evident, His wisdom appeared, and reality conformed to what He reported. Furthermore, parables are only given through sensible things, and these are either heavenly or earthly; so the bringing into existence of these beings is only for the sake of knowledge of God, exalted is He.

Since the intended meaning of "the worlds" may be obscure, he clarified it with his saying, using emphasis to indicate that their condition in not benefiting from reflection upon them is like the condition of one who denies that there is any indication in them: ﴿Indeed, in that﴾, meaning: in that great matter of their reflecting on the conformity of reality to His report, glory be to Him, so He reports nothing except that reality, from them both or from what is in them, conforms to it, exactly equal, ﴿is a sign﴾, meaning: an indication that brings happiness, ﴿for the believers﴾, meaning: those who are in truth the knowledgeable. Their knowledge of the benefits in both realms that follow from the known order drives them, together with the wonder of their very creation despite the greatness of their bodies and the marvel of their precise design, to belief in all that He has reported, until they have no kind of doubt at all, and it becomes for them a quality that does not depart.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 45:

When this entire report had conveyed the Qur'an, which is the truth than which no truth is greater, and indicated that understanding its like requires an increase of knowledge, and that the key to knowledge of it, glorified is He, is the firmness of faith, He addressed the head of the people of faith, because he is the greatest of those who understand it, so that the followers might take him as their model, and said: (p-447) ﴿Recite what﴾, that is: continue its recitation. He indicated its nobility by singling him out with His words ﴿has been revealed to you﴾, since wahy (revelation) is a secret casting [of speech], ﴿from the Book﴾ [that is:] the one that gathers every good, for it is what produces faith, together with the fact that it is the truest of truths for the sake of which the heavens and the earth were created. Frequent recitation of it increases insight into its matter and opens the treasures of its subtle meanings. It is too noble to grant its reciter a benefit and too majestic to yield the reins of its fruits or lift the veil from its jewels and pearls at the first time. Rather, whenever the reciter repeats it with reflection, it bestows upon him a treasure of its secrets, and however much he increases, it increases him in the flashing of its lights, until he is certain that its wonders cannot be counted and its strange features cannot be bounded.

When He had guided to the key of knowledge, He indicated the rule of action, which cannot be sound except through the Qur'an, and it is that which gathers resolve, so the heart becomes present, the breast is expanded, and thought is set in motion within the gardens of its sciences. So He said: ﴿And establish the prayer﴾, that is, the one which is the most worthy of the acts of worship. Then He gave the reason for that with His words, emphasizing by means of the particle of emphasis the greatness of its matter and that it is among things hidden from most people: ﴿Indeed, the prayer forbids﴾, that is, it brings about prohibition and renews it for one who is constant in establishing it with all its limits, ﴿from immorality﴾, that is, the traits whose ugliness has reached its extreme, ﴿and wrongdoing﴾, that is, that in which there is some kind of ugliness, however subtle. The least of what it contains of prohibition is the prohibition against abandoning it, which is disbelief. Whoever refrains from that (p-448) has his breast expanded and his thought widened, so he knows of the secrets of the Qur'an what no one else knows. ﴿And fear Allah; and Allah teaches you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282].

Since the one who truly forbids is none other than the remembrance of Allah, He followed this with an exhortation to the spirit of prayer and its greatest purpose, which is watchfulness over the One to whom one prays, until it is as if one sees Him, so that by this one may attain the greatest remembrance, with His words: ﴿And the remembrance of Allah﴾, that is: and because the remembrance of the One who deserves every attribute of perfection ﴿is greater﴾, that is, greater than everything. Whoever brings that to mind in his heart finds everything other than Him trivial in his sight. [It is in the hadith:] "Indeed, My servant, every servant of Mine, is the one who remembers Me at the meeting of his opponent." Or the meaning may be that whoever persists in prayer remembers Allah, and whoever remembers Him is near to having his heart softened, and whoever has his heart softened has his intellect illuminated, so this remembrance, which bears this fruit, is near to forbidding him from disobedience. Thus the remembrance of the one who remembers Him, glorified is He, is greater in forbidding him from wrongdoing than the prayer's forbidding him. And his remembrance of Him, glorified is He, is great, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So remember Me; I will remember you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 152]. If this is the state of the servant's remembrance of his Master, then what do you think of his Master's remembrance of him whenever he turns to Him in prayer? He is worthy to raise him to a degree that cannot be described, and to clothe him with garments of His lights that cannot be enumerated.

(p-449) Since that requires treatment for crooked natures and deviant temperaments, training in arduous burdens, and taming of the souls' restiveness, and since he (ﷺ) had been purified of all of that by what he was made disposed to from the origin of natural disposition, and then by what He washed his heart with of the water of wisdom, [and other than that] of the sublime blessing, he turned to addressing the followers, urging them to striving, and said: ﴿And Allah﴾, that is, the One encompassing in knowledge and power, ﴿knows﴾, that is, at every time, ﴿what you do﴾ of good and evil, expressing it with the term "ṣun'ah" (doing/making), which indicates constancy of practice, as an alert that establishing what was mentioned requires constant training and drilling, until it becomes a sound disposition and a clear, deliberate aim.

The discourse has now reached the spirit of religion and the secret of certainty, which no one knows truly except the scholars of the heavenly Books and the divine reports. The scholar is able to raise doubts and circulate dubious arguments, so that a single doubt may lead astray the heedless among people, because of the acceptance he enjoys among them, because souls are inclined toward falsehoods, and because of Satan's embellishment in this. Disputation begets enmity and opens the doors of trials, and so leads to error. God, Exalted, said, linking to ﴿Recite﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 45], addressing whoever concluded the verse with their address, to exalt his station (ﷺ) above confrontation of this kind, and as a warning that he should not direct his noble resolve to such things, because disputation, contention and contesting are not in his nature: ﴿And do not dispute with the People of the Book﴾, that is, the Jews and the Christians, thinking that disputation benefits the religion, or increases certainty, or turns anyone away from manifest error, ﴿except in the way that is best﴾, that is, by the recitation of the Revelation, which We commanded the chief of the worshippers to keep reciting alone. This is as mentioned earlier at His saying, Exalted, in Subhan: ﴿And tell My servants to say that which is best﴾ [al-Isra': 53].

Since everyone among them who disputed about the Qur'an was a wrongdoer, it is clear that those excepted in His saying, ﴿except those of them who have done wrong﴾, are those who exceeded in wrongdoing by denying the soundness of the Qur'an and denying its inimitability, for example, and by claiming it is in the style of the earlier Books, or that it confirms something of them, or by their saying, ﴿God has not sent down anything to a human﴾ [al-An'am: 91], and similar of their fabrications. Disputing with these is permitted, even if it leads to their being struck with the sword, for the religion prevails and is not overcome.

Since He forbade the cause of disagreement, He commanded conciliation, saying: ﴿And say: We believe﴾, that is, we affirm belief ﴿in what has been sent down to us﴾, that is, from this inimitable Book, ﴿and what has been sent down to you﴾ from your Books, meaning that its origin is true, even though some of it has been abrogated (naskh), and what they tell you of anything that you have no knowledge of, neither confirming nor denying it, then do not believe them nor disbelieve them, for this is more conducive to fairness and more effective in averting disagreement.

Since this does not comprise both parties, He followed it with what unites them, saying: ﴿Our God and your God is One﴾. Since it is certain that what is meant by Him is God, because Muslims do not worship other than Him, and since all the sects acknowledge divinity, even if in some form of acknowledgment, [need] does not call for saying "God" as in the rest of the verses, so He said: ﴿One﴾, meaning there is no god for us other than Him, even if some of you claim Ezra and the Messiah. ﴿And to Him we are submitting﴾ exclusively, ﴿Muslims﴾, that is, subservient and obedient in the fullest submission to what He commands us, after the foundations, in the branches of law, whether they agree with your branches, like facing Bayt al-Maqdis in prayer, or abrogate them, like facing the Ka'bah. And we do not take the rabbis and monks as lords besides God, so that we would take what they legislate for us in opposition to His Book and the Sunnah of His Prophet (ﷺ), for then we would have submitted to them and been arrogant toward Him, and thus we would have placed Islam in other than its proper place, by injustice.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 47:

Since the implied meaning was a justification for the command to say this statement, namely, "We have sent down their scriptures to their messengers," he joined to it his saying, addressing the head (of the Prophets) specifically, so that no critic would find an opening to attack the generality or to accuse the one to whom it was revealed (p-452): ﴿And thus﴾, i.e., in the same manner as that revelation which We sent down to their prophets, ﴿We have sent down to you the Book﴾, i.e., this Qur'an, which is truly "the Book," with no other book being equal to it in the sublimity of its perfection, in its composition and its speech, ﴿confirming what is before it﴾. ﴿Those to whom﴾, i.e., it follows from Our sending it down in this way, that those ﴿We have given﴾ [i.e., ] a giving befitting Our greatness, so that they came to recognize truth from falsehood, ﴿the Book﴾, i.e., previously, ﴿believe in it﴾, i.e., in this Book, in reality, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and Mukhayriq, may Allah be pleased with both of them, or figuratively, through knowing it while disbelieving, such as Huyayy ibn Akhtab and many others among them. ﴿And among these﴾, i.e., the Arabs, ﴿are those who believe in it﴾, i.e., likewise, in reality and figuratively, through inwardly knowing that it is true because of the proof it established of that by their inability to oppose it, while disbelieving in it. The strongest evidence for what you intended regarding the real and the figurative is His saying: ﴿And none deny﴾, i.e., none of the two groups deny after knowing it. Al-Baghawi said: Qatadah said: denial only occurs after knowledge.

﴿Our signs﴾, which have attained the utmost ends of greatness, so that they deserve to be attributed to Us, ﴿except the disbelievers﴾, i.e., those who persist in concealing the knowledge after its manifestation, hoping to extinguish its light.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 48:

(p-453) When he had indicated that the one who denies the very origin of revelation is deeply immersed in disbelief, he demonstrated this through the condition of the one to whom it was sent down, ﷺ, saying, consoling him: ﴿Nor] wouldst thou have recited] before it any Book, nor wouldst thou have written it with thy right hand. That is: We sent it down to you while you were not one who ﴿recited﴾, i.e., read continuously and persistently at any time.

Since the intent was to negate recitation over both a long and a short span of past time, he introduced the preposition, saying ﴿before it﴾, i.e., before this Book which We sent down to you. He also emphasized the comprehensiveness regarding books, saying ﴿any Book﴾ at all, ﴿nor wouldst thou have written it﴾, i.e., you did not renew or persist in its writing. He depicted the writing and emphasized it by saying ﴿with thy right hand﴾, i.e., the one which is the stronger of the two limbs. He expressed it this way to indicate that doubt about his matter could not arise in any intelligent person except through persistent practice of such activities with strong persistence, from which a faculty is produced; how much more so when the very act itself has not occurred. For this reason He said ﴿Otherwise﴾, i.e., if any of this persistence in recitation or writing, through which habit is acquired that inherits the faculty, had existed, ﴿the falsifiers would have had cause for doubt﴾, i.e., it would have been possible for these falsifiers to be driven into doubt, namely those who deny the revelation to you, from among the People of the Book and from among the Arabs, who say: it is rhymed prose, soothsaying, poetry, and tales of the ancients. They are the ones firmly rooted in describing falsehood, i.e., entering into falsehood (p-454), so they would find a point of attack. The Arabs would say: "Perhaps he took it from the books of the ancients." And the People of the Book would say: "The one announced in our scriptures is unlettered, yet there was neither reading nor writing in him, as is well known of your condition, let alone persistence in either of them." Thus there is no doubt about your truthfulness in ascribing it to God, the Exalted. And when doubt is removed from its root, it is correct to negate what they hold of it, because, since there was in reality no basis for them, their doubt was counted as nonexistent. They were called falsifiers on the assumption of this supposed doubt, since the remaining decisive miracles establishing the message, which judge for truthfulness, stand just as they judged for the truthfulness of their own prophets, [even though] they used to write and read, and their books were not sent down as a miracle. So it is established that they are bound to be characterized as falsifiers through doubt under every assumption of the two cases, writing and reading, and their absence, because the mainstay rests upon the miracles.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 49:

Since the implied sense is: "Rather, they have no doubt at all, nor any suspicion, regarding it, for their saying that it is falsehood," He said: ﴿Rather, it﴾, that is, the Qur'an which you brought and about which they doubted, so that they are wrongdoers in that regard under every assumption, ﴿is clear signs﴾, that is, evident proofs, ﴿clear﴾, that is, very manifest in indicating your truthfulness, ﴿in the breasts of those who﴾. Since the intent is to emphasize the greatness of knowledge, the verb was put in the passive form and the thing whose original form would be a pronoun was made explicit, so He said: ﴿have been given knowledge﴾, indicating that it is complete, beneficial knowledge, so no one can distort any part of it to obscure the truth to them. In this there is an indication that its being hidden from others has no effect. And since the knowledge intended is beneficial knowledge, He said (p-455), indicating that in the breasts of others it is devoid of benefit: ﴿And none deny﴾. The original form would have been "it," but He pointed to its greatness and said: ﴿Our signs﴾, that is, they reject them after knowing them, given their greatness by attributing them to Us, [and the clear evidence which no one denies]. ﴿except the wrongdoers﴾, that is, those firmly established in wrongdoing, who do not benefit from their light in placing each thing in its proper place; rather, they place things in other than their proper place, like one walking in darkness, which resulted from their first attribute of disbelief, which is covering the lights of the intellects.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 50:

Since the implied sense is: they denied them [with the firm entrenchment in wrongdoing that they had] entirely and utterly, and did not regard them as signs, let alone as clear proofs, he joined to it His saying: ﴿And they said﴾, feigning cunning and a display of fairness by being content with the least that indicates truthfulness: ﴿Why has not﴾, that is, "Why not" (hallā), ﴿a sign been sent down to him﴾, that is, in whatever manner of sending down it may be, ﴿from his Lord﴾, that is, from the One whom he claims has bestowed favour upon him, as was sent down to the prophets before him, such as the she-camel of Ṣāliḥ, the staff of Mūsā, and the like, ﴿so that we may take proof from it of the truth of his speech and the soundness of what he claims about his condition.﴾ This is the reading of Ibn Kathīr [and] Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī and Abū Bakr, in the singular; the others read it in the plural, indicating that another group said: "Such a grave and important matter is not established except by multiple signs," and they gave the impression, out of arrogance and obstinacy, that this had not happened, even if something called a sign had occurred. (p-456)

Since this was a denial of the sun after its rising, and an arrogant rejection of the miracles with which he challenged them after their certainty, He indicated it by His saying: ﴿Say﴾, that is, to them, giving them free rein until it is as if you had brought them nothing: ﴿The signs are only with Allah﴾, that is, the One to whom all command belongs, so none other than Him can send down any of them; for the true God is He alone, with no other. ﴿And I am only a warner﴾, who stands up for you with what He has charged and obligated me with of warning, showing this by the signs I have been given and by breaking the habitual patterns; and it is not for me to propose signs [to Him]. Moreover, the aim of a sign is to show truthfulness, and all of them are in the ruling of one sign in that respect [and it was not necessary to mention the good news, because it is not its style]. ﴿Clear﴾, that is, the clearest of what I have brought of that, after having made clear the soundness of my being a warner; so the sending down of signs is not up to me, nor is requesting them a matter of proposing them to Allah. This is a qalb (reversal) restriction in both respects, addressed to one who is bound to claim that the sending down of signs is up to the Prophet ﷺ and that his task is to bring whatever they wish or ask of him.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 51:

When [the Qur'an] had gladdened them with what [it said], as if it were an acceptance of their claim, and it was clear that the tongue of the situation says: "Were they not sufficed by the signs I brought them, the visible and the audible ones, when they were unable to produce anything like them?", He followed this with His words, rebuking their ignorance (p-457) and obstinacy: ﴿Is it not sufficient for them﴾, that is, if they were seekers of the truth and not contentious, ﴿that We have sent down﴾ by Our majesty ﴿to you the Book﴾, that is, the one that gathers the happiness of both abodes, to such a degree that it has become your disposition, predominant over your movements and your stillness, ﴿being recited to them﴾, that is, its recitation is continually renewed upon them, bit by bit, in every place and every time, by every reciter, confirming what is in the earlier scriptures of your description and other signs that indicate your truthfulness. They are challenged by everything that has been revealed from it, together with the challenge by what came before it of its signs, morning and evening. Through this they are struck on the nape of the neck throughout the ages, and they push back; whenever they wish to advance, they are thrown back by their incapacity. How great, then, is this as a lasting sign, since every other sign has passed away and gone by.

[And Shaykh Abu al-'Abbas al-Mursi said: Some of the Companions, may God be pleased with them, were moved to humility upon hearing the Jews recite the Torah, so they were blamed for becoming humble at other than the Qur'an, though they were only humbled by the Torah, which is the speech of God. So what do you suppose of one who turns away from the Book of God and is humbled by frivolities and singing?]

Since this is greater than every sign they could propose, even if its signs continued to come to them every day, because this [Qur'an] endures through the passing of days and months until ages and eras come to an end, (p-458) the Exalted pointed to this greatness, along with the blessing it contains, in His words, emphasizing their ignorance regarding what followed from their first speech, namely their denial that there could be in the Qur'an a sign that would guide them to truthfulness: ﴿Indeed in that﴾, that is, the sending down of the Book in this manner, far-reaching in attainment and wondrous in its example, ﴿is surely a mercy﴾ for them, because it polishes the rust of hearts at every moment and purifies the impurity of souls at every glance, ﴿and a reminder﴾, that is, a great reminder, continuously [being remembered].

Since He generalized in speech, He then specified in terms of benefit, saying: ﴿for a people who believe﴾, that is, for whom it is possible that faith may newly arise, and whose concern is not obstinacy. Al-Hirali said in a book of his on the foundations of religion: Since the Qur'an is a tongue of comprehensiveness, no creature of God has been able to fulfil it, because it is built upon the universal totality of God's command, to the extent that a single surah of it, when its address is directed at it from the spans of its construction upon the comprehensiveness of God's command, no creature can produce it. And if the least of the speech of a scholar cannot be produced by one below his rank, then the incapacity of creatures before the speech of God is more worthy and more fitting. Then every one who looks into it, from whatever aspect he looks, perceives by the requirement of its elevation over his own rank an aspect of incapacity in it. If he is eloquent and rhetorical, then it is from the aspect of eloquence (balaghah), whose meaning is the speech reaching the fullest correspondence with its information, which is called fasahah (clarity), and the beauty of the arrangement of the letters of its words, which is called jazalah (vigour), and the perfection of the coherence of its words and verses, which is called husn al-nazm (beauty of arrangement), reaching its furthest ends and most complete conclusions. If he is a scholar of the reports of the earlier peoples, then it is by the soundness of what they require in it. If he is wise, then it is by the most complete information on the manner in which consequences follow from their causes. In sum, no one possesses a root of intellect or a share of knowledge, of whatever kind, without finding a place for it in the Qur'an, which fulfils for it a share of exposition of the exalted rank of its reports, at a perceived limit of it, to a degree about whose occurrence there is no doubt, above the level of creatures. Thus it is a lasting and enduring sign. The first hearer of it does not differ in receiving it from the last hearer in the manner of hearing it. Every prophet's sign has been lost with his passing, or with the passing of the time when it appeared at his hands, but the sign of Muhammad (ﷺ) remains as long as God remains. So the aspects by which its miraculousness appears come upon the shares of the kinds of creatures from the modes of perception. No particular aspect is fixed for the manifestation of its inimitability, and no observer who looks into it loses a share through which, according to the measure of his perception, he may arrive at certainty about the mode of its inimitability. This is because it encompasses every detail and every generality, and it has omitted nothing, and because it is an elaboration of everything and, by its comprehensiveness in establishing every rank of the wisdom of God, the Exalted, no creature, whether among jinn, humans, red or black [peoples], or all of God's creation, whether those whom people know among them or those unknown to them, who are encompassed by the knowledge of the worlds through God's informing, is able to hold back from believing in it. From the judgement of the comprehensiveness of His Book, it was possible for every high sign that a prophet before him brought, from among those who witnessed it, to be transmitted by those present, and transmitted through tawatur (mass transmission) and istifadah (widespread reporting) by the bearers of knowledge, generation after generation. Then he arranged an analogy on the proof of prophethood, saying: Muhammad (ﷺ) possesses a sign, this Qur'an that is witnessed, and this witnessed Qur'an is inimitable to every person of perception, and a good tidings from every aspect of its meanings and its eloquence. So the possessor of this Qur'an's sign is a prophet, and Muhammad (ﷺ) [is a prophet]. As for Muhammad (ﷺ) possessing its sign, it is by the certain auditory experience called tawatur. As for this Qur'an being inimitable, it is in what every observer finds in its meaning, which includes the complete wisdom concerning what exists, the account of what was before, and the report of what will be after, with certainty that its beginnings occur as its whole occurs, and the soundness of its report. Through this it becomes clear that the possessor of its sign is a prophet. Then through what it contains of its testimony to the possessor of its sign and its explicit declaration of this concerning Muhammad (ﷺ), it is established that Muhammad (ﷺ) possesses its sign and that he is a prophet (ﷺ). The reasoning used in this is that Muhammad (ﷺ) challenged the eloquent and stubborn Arabs, the skilled rhetoricians, with this Qur'an. When they resorted to war, it became clear that they fled to that place because of the incapacity they found in themselves. If those [eloquent ones] were incapable, then those after them are even more deserving of incapacity. When incapacity encompassed all creatures, (p-461) it became necessary to know that this Qur'an is true, and that the one who challenged with it is a prophet who came with truth. Its essence is this: had the Arabs not been incapable, they would not have waged war, with the heaviness of war and the lightness of opposition, if they had been able to do it; and since they did not oppose [with words] but waged war, they were incapable. Thus it is established that he is a prophet (ﷺ). End of quotation.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 52:

Since it is known that they say, "We do not believe that this Book is from Allah, let alone that we would be content with it," He said: ﴿Say﴾, i.e., as a response to what they may say of this kind: ﴿Allah is sufficient﴾, i.e., the One who possesses all greatness and all other perfections, who has borne witness to me concerning the prophethood in His Book, the Book whose being His speech He established by the inability of creation to produce its like.

Since the concern in this surah is with mentioning people and detailing their conditions, He began with His saying ﴿between me and you﴾ before His saying ﴿as a witness﴾, unlike in Surah al-Ra'd and Surah al-An'am. Then He described the Witness, or gave the reason for His sufficiency, with His saying ﴿He knows what is in the heavens﴾, i.e., all of them. And since the earth has no other than this one which they witness, He mentioned it in the singular in the context of the coming of the revelation and the Qur'an from it, saying: ﴿and the earth﴾, i.e., nothing of that is hidden from Him. So He is Knowing of what they attribute to me of fabricating against Him, and of what I attribute to Him from this Qur'an, through which your inability to match it has borne witness for me. So He is a witness for me. In reality, Allah is the One who witnesses for me, by what is in it of praise of me and testimony to my truthfulness, because the Qur'an's being His speech has been established by the inability to produce its like, and the falsifying of the falsifier among us will be made manifest by reason.

Since the sense is: "And you know that He has borne witness for me that I am upon the truth, and that everything that opposes what I have brought is falsehood, so those who believe in the truth and disbelieve in falsehood are the successful ones," He followed this with His saying: ﴿And those who believe in falsehood﴾, i.e., in what it is not permissible to believe in, from every deity other than Allah, ﴿and disbelieve in Allah﴾, whom it is obligatory to believe in and to be grateful to, because to Him belongs all perfection, and everything other than Him is perishing, having of itself nothing but non-existence. ﴿Those﴾ are the distant and the hateful; ﴿they﴾, i.e., specifically, ﴿are the losers﴾, i.e., the most complete in loss, for they have lost themselves forever.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 53:

Since their saying, once, "Why has no sign been sent down upon him?" was a matter of wonder, [Allah] followed the report of their loss with something more wondrous than it, namely the persistence of their urging for what lies beyond any power of theirs, of the punishment of Allah. So He said: ﴿And they urge you to hasten the punishment﴾, meaning, they demand that you hasten it at every time, ﴿the punishment﴾, and they make its delay from them a doubt for them in what they claim of denial. ﴿And were it not for a term appointed﴾, which has been set for the time of their punishment, with no advancing or delaying in it, ﴿the punishment would have come upon them﴾ at the time of their urging, because power is complete and knowledge encompasses.

(p-463) Since this has made clear that it must certainly come, he stated it explicitly in His saying, emphasising it as a rejection of their mockery which contains denial: ﴿And it will surely come upon them﴾. Then He magnified it by His saying: ﴿suddenly﴾, and He emphasised its meaning by His saying: ﴿while they do not perceive﴾, rather they are in the utmost heedlessness of it and occupied with what makes them forget it.

Then he increased the expression of wonder at their ignorance with his saying, in apposition: ﴿They ask you to hasten the punishment﴾, i.e., they demand of you that it be inflicted upon them immediately, even though it is not at its most fitting time. So if they knew what they are heading toward, they would wish that they had never been created, let alone that they hasten it, and they would exert their whole effort to escape from it.

Since their entry into the Fire was necessary, given that the power (of God) encompasses them, He said, emphasizing against their denial of the Hereafter by affirming something more specific than it: ﴿And indeed Hell﴾, which is part of the punishment of the Hereafter, ﴿is surely encompassing﴾, i.e., by what is prepared for it, since nothing of it escapes, because the One who prepared it is All-Knowing and All-Powerful. And He said ﴿the disbelievers﴾ in place of "them", as a warning about what made them deserve its punishment, and as a generalization to include everyone who is characterized by it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 55:

When all of this served as evidence of their denial, He said: ﴿On the Day﴾, meaning: they will know that [on the Day] ﴿the punishment will envelop them﴾, meaning: it will reach them and cling to them, leaving them nothing they could find sweet, nor any matter they could enjoy. He drew attention to the fact that the direction of above does not wholly encompass them, despite its being higher than them, by affirming the preposition, so He said: ﴿from above them﴾. Since this implied encompassing what is lower than the direction of above, He stated it explicitly, saying: ﴿and from beneath their feet﴾. Thus it became known that He encompasses them from all sides. He stated "feet" explicitly to affirm the human (ādamī) condition. ﴿And He will say﴾, meaning: God, according to the reading of Nafi', 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i with the yā' (third-person), following the past-tense style; or "We, in Our majesty," according to the reading of the rest, as a way of alarming them by turning to the manifestation of majesty: ﴿Taste﴾ what He has caused for you, ﴿what you used to﴾ do with utmost eagerness ﴿do﴾, meaning: on that Day you will know this with the knowledge of certainty (ḥaqq al-yaqīn) after your knowledge of it was merely the knowledge of sight (ʿayn al-yaqīn), because of your denial with the knowledge of certainty ('ilm al-yaqīn).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 56:

When he had given the warning thoroughly, and cautioned against the great matters, and had not neglected to allude to the minor ones, and these verses were addressed to the obstinate among the disbelievers, and he had repeatedly made clear that these admonitions are only for the believers, he addressed them directly, turning away from others, since their ears had attended to the eloquent admonitions and their hearts had awakened to the weighty warnings. It is an iltifat (shift of grammatical person), according to the recitation of the majority, to the delight of intimate communion in singling them out and drawing them away from the avenues of obstinacy: ﴿O My servants﴾. He thus honoured them with the possessive attribution. But since he indicated with the particle of distance that among them are those who had not taken firm root, he confirmed this with His words: ﴿who have believed﴾ [i.e.: ] even though faith by the tongue alone accompanied by the least portion of the heart is still faith.

When this surah was revealed in Makkah, and they were there concealing their worship out of fear of the disbelievers, and emigration from one's family and homeland was difficult, he said, emphasising it as an alert that the state of one who abandons emigration is the state of one who thinks the earth is narrow: ﴿Indeed My earth is spacious﴾, i.e., in terms of provision and everything you desire of ease. So if you cannot manage, because of these obstinate people who tempt you in your religion and prevent you from sincerely devoting [to Me] in your land and striving in My worship until faith becomes an attribute of yours, then emigrate to a land where you can attain that.

Since residence there before the conquest led to temptation, and the one who is tempted may comply with his tongue, and that, although the heart is at peace with faith, takes the form of polytheism, He said: ﴿So Me alone﴾, i.e., specifically by emigrating to a land where you will be secure, ﴿worship﴾, and take heed, ﴿so worship Me﴾, by reason of the benefits I have arranged for you, such as expanding the earth and other things, worship free of any association, neither with the tongue nor otherwise, nor with contempt for it, nor out of regard for a creature in disobedience to Him, nor with anything that draws one toward it by fleeing from one who prevents you from it to one who helps you to it.

(p-466) Since emigration (al-hijrah) is very bitter, because in meaning it involves leaving what is familiar and beloved: kin, homeland, and wealth, and death includes all of that with something more, He said, emphasizing this, reminding of it, and instilling dread of abandoning emigration: ﴿Every soul shall taste death﴾, that is, the separation from everything it has become accustomed to, even the body which it has long clothed itself in, and which it has been intimate with and which has been intimate with it. So if it obeys its Lord, it saves its soul, and obedience does not diminish its term (ajal) in the slightest; and if not, it destroys its soul, and disobedience does not increase its term in the slightest. Thus, when a person considers that he has died, emigration becomes easy for him, for if he does not part with some of what is familiar to him through it, he parts with all that is familiar to him [by death]. The mention of death never occurs in a matter of hardship without making it easy for him, and never in a matter of ease without making it difficult for him and troubling it.

Since he made light the matter of emigration, he warned those who are content, in their religion, with some kind of deficiency in something, urging them to prepare with utmost effort by provisioning themselves for the return: so He said: ﴿Then to Us you will be returned﴾, to Our majesty, not to other than Us, ﴿you will be returned﴾ in the easiest manner, and He will recompense each of you for what he has done.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 58:

When the implied sense is: "As for those who believe and then cloak their faith with some kind of deficiency, We will diminish their recompense; and as for those who disbelieve, We will cast them down in Hell into levels beneath levels, ﴿so wretched is the abode of the wrongdoers﴾," but the mention of punishment has just preceded, and the intent here is to encourage faith in whatever form it takes, he omitted this and indicated it by coupling to it His words: ﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾, meaning: as confirmation of their faith, ﴿righteous deeds﴾, meaning: all of them.

Since the disbelievers denied the Resurrection, and what follows it, he emphasised His words: ﴿We will surely settle them﴾, meaning: We will surely lodge them in a place worthy that one should return to it, because of its goodness and pleasantness, from which one has gone out for some of one's needs. This is the meaning of: ﴿in the Garden, lofty chambers﴾, meaning: high houses beneath which are wide, splendid, lofty halls. Close to this meaning is the reading of Hamzah and al-Kisa'i with the letter thāʾ (ث) pointed from *thawā*, meaning to dwell in a place when one stays in it.

Since lofty places are not made pleasant except by gardens, he said: ﴿flowing﴾. And since the general nature of water is toward the lower direction, in relation to punishment, he resembled [the pleasure] by specifying it, saying: ﴿beneath them rivers﴾. It is well known that wherever there are rivers there are also large gardens, crops, meadows and flowers, so they look down upon them from those lofty places.

Since they will be in a state in which there is no distress that would require leaving it for even a moment, he alluded to this by His words: ﴿abiding therein﴾, meaning: they will not seek any change from it. Then he magnified its matter and honoured its rank by His words: ﴿How excellent is the reward of those who act.﴾

Then He described them with what encourages emigration, saying, defining the sum of all good as patience and that it is by way of entrusting oneself to God, (p-468) alerting that a person is never free of some arduous matter that patience must be exercised upon: ﴿Those who endure patiently﴾, meaning: they brought this reality into being until it settled within them and became their innate disposition, so they applied it to every arduous obligation, such as emigration and others.

Since a person inclines more toward the one who does him good, He said, encouraging rest in entrusting oneself to Him: ﴿And upon their Lord﴾, meaning: Him alone, not upon family or homeland, ﴿they rely﴾, meaning: [they bring about reliance continuously renewed at every important matter that confronts them] regarding their provision after emigration and otherwise, their striving against their enemies, and other of their affairs.

When he (Allah) mentioned reliance (tawakkul) upon Him as sufficient in the matter of provision, both at home and abroad, with neither wealth nor family, He said, linking this to what is implied by its context: "How many a one who relies upon Him has He sufficed, and has not made him in need of anyone else. Let him hasten, whoever He has rescued from disbelief and guided to emigration, seeking His pleasure." ﴿And how many a creature does not carry its provision﴾, meaning: many of the creatures, rational and otherwise, ﴿do not carry﴾, meaning: are not able to carry ﴿its provision﴾, and do not store anything for a later hour, because it may not perceive the benefit of that, or it may perceive it and rely (on Allah), or it may not find (food).

Since the place of the question "Then who provides for it?" was reached, He answered it: ﴿Allah﴾, meaning: the One who encompasses all knowledge and power, who is characterized by every perfection, ﴿provides for it﴾ although it does not store, ﴿and you﴾ although you store. There is no difference between His provision for it despite its weakness and His provision for you despite your strength and your storing, for both groups sometimes find and sometimes do not find. Thus storing and not storing become of no account and not something to be regarded.

Since the most important concern of an animal is provision, it is never free from managing it, with what occurs to its heart and what it expresses if it is speaking, and what it murmurs if it is silent. As for the rational person, his concern is with universal matters; as for other than him, it is with particular, singular things. And since the rational person may say, "I am not able to cut off these attachments," He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And He is the All-Hearing﴾, meaning: of whatever can be heard concerning His affairs and other than His affairs, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾, meaning: of what He knows of that, and of what your affair and the affair of your enemy will come to. He has not commanded you with what He commanded you except that He has prepared its means for it. He is able to cause the means that a person relies upon to produce their effect, and to ensure that what hinders them is removed, and He is able to cause for the one who relies upon Him and severs attachments what will suffice him. Whoever reads the books of Sufism (tasawwuf), the biographies of the people, and the lives of the early generations (al-salaf) — may Allah benefit us through them — will find much of this, which enlightens him, consoles him, and makes him patient, glory be to Him.

When He, glory be to Him, made the matter of provision easy by addressing the believers, after He had thoroughly admonished the disbelievers through clear speech, the striking of parables, and gentle argument in disputation, and since a king cannot fully control the provision of those outside his kingdom, He said, [linking to the sense of: "If you asked them about that, they would surely confirm it for you"] (p. 470), returning to the solicitation of those who turn away and kindness toward the heedless, following the method of wisdom (hikmah) in the varied forms of admonition. This is like a master who has two servants, one righteous and one corrupt. He advises the corrupt one, and if he does not listen, the master turns to the righteous one, turning away from the corrupt one and saying, "This one does not deserve to be addressed. Listen, you, and do not be like him." His words thus contain both counsel to the righteous one and rebuke to the corrupt one. Then, when the corrupt one hears the admonition given to his brother, this moves him after the earlier stirring by the turning away and the reproach, through his bad view of himself and his lack of insight. So when the master addresses him after this, he finds him prepared to accept, inclined toward agreement, and repelled by opposition: ﴿And if you asked them﴾, that is, the believer and others, though the intended reference is chiefly to him: ﴿who created the heavens and the earth﴾ and what lies beyond them, in this great order, ﴿and subjected the sun and the moon﴾ for the regulation of sustenance, the knowledge of times, and other benefits.

Since their state in denying the resurrection is like the state of one who denies that He, glory be to Him, created this existence, He emphasized it as an alert that acknowledging this entails acknowledging the resurrection, and so He said: ﴿They will surely say, "Allah"﴾, that is, the One who possesses all attributes of perfection, because this is firmly established in their natural dispositions (fitar) and they received it from their forefathers, in agreement with the truth in reality.

Since the state of one whose aspiration is turned away from Him is strange and deserves to be asked about, in the manner of wonder at him, indicating that there is no justification for it, He said: ﴿So how﴾, that is, how and in what manner, ﴿are they deflected﴾, that is, turned away by a turner, those who do not rely upon Him or do not devote worship sincerely to Him in all their states, and in all their sayings and actions, from sincerity toward Him, despite their acknowledgment that He has no partner in creation. Thus their face is turned to their back, so they see things contrary to what they are, and they fall into blundering like a blind camel and into the bewilderment of a lost wanderer.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 62:

Since the disparity in provision may be puzzling to everyone who has not reflected with due reflection, and it may be said: "All creation and provision belong to Him, so why are they unequal in provision?" He said: ﴿Allah﴾, that is, with what He has of greatness (al-'azamah) and encompassing of the attributes of perfection, ﴿expands provision﴾ by His perfect power ﴿for whom He wills of His servants﴾ according to what He knows of their inner states, ﴿and restricts it﴾, that is, He constricts it.

Since that [expansion and restriction] is for the welfare of the servants, even if the wisdom behind it does not appear to them, He said: ﴿for Him﴾, that is, so that through it His power and His wisdom may become manifest. You see kings and others among the powerful distributing provision unequally among their workers according to what they know from their limited knowledge of their circumstances. So what do you suppose of the King of kings, whose knowledge is such that doubts and uncertainties do not approach His court? This verse is the consequence of what precedes it.

Since He, glorified is He, provides for people, and it is possible for them, according to what He knows of their inner selves (p-472), that there is no welfare except in it, He said, giving the reason for that and emphasizing it in rebuttal of those who believe that this disparity is only due to the negligence of some servants and the diligence of others, informing that He is all-encompassing in knowledge, and therefore all-encompassing in power; He is the One who caused the incapacity of some of them and the capacity of others, since power necessarily entails knowledge: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, that is, the One who possesses the attributes of perfection, ﴿of everything﴾ [that is:] of those who are provided for and of provisions, and how they are withheld or driven, and other things, ﴿is All-Knowing﴾. So He is capable of all of that; He knows what benefits the servants in this matter and what corrupts them, and He gives them according to that, if He wills. How often some of the powerful have sought to make a poor man rich or a rich man poor, but He exposed the condition of the corruption of what they sought of change.

Once the comprehensiveness of His knowledge was established by this, it necessarily follows that His power is complete, as He proved in Ta-Ha. So He said, pointing to that and mentioning the near cause of provision after mentioning the distant one, since acknowledging that this cause comes from Him necessarily entails acknowledging that the effect also comes from Him: ﴿And if you asked them, "Who sent down"﴾ gradually, in accordance with [what He did] in provision. [And since a claimant might assert that he extracted water and brought it down from a mountain or the like, He mentioned what belongs exclusively to Him, free from the claims of claimants, and said]: ﴿water from the sky﴾, after it had been held in the realm of height, ﴿and revived﴾ [And since most of the earth comes to life through rainwater without need of irrigation, He put the preposition first and said]: ﴿with it the earth﴾, the dusty one. By including the preposition, He indicated the nearness of growth to the time of death, [and that they do not know beyond the existing, sensible particulars, and their intellects do not penetrate to the intelligible universals with the penetration of the people of faith, so that they would know that what He, glory be to Him, brings into existence actually at a time, it exists either by His bringing it into being when He wills. So the earth is alive by His giving it life, glory be to Him, through the cause of rain, throughout the entire period that comes after death potentially, just as it is alive in part actually]. So He said: ﴿after its death﴾, and it became green, stirring, after there had been nothing of that in it. He emphasized, for the sake of the same warning given earlier, that their condition in denying resurrection is the condition of one who denies that God is the Maker of this, because the power to do it entails the power to resurrect, [by His saying]: ﴿They will surely say, "God."﴾ And He, in whom is all perfection, so their monotheism became obligatory for them.

Since it was established that He is the Creator, both at the beginning and in restoration, as is witnessed in every age, He said, alerting to the greatness of His attributes, the necessary consequence of affirming them being the truthfulness of His Messenger ﷺ: ﴿Say﴾, marveling at them for their obstinacy, since they acknowledge what obliges them to monotheism and then do not affirm monotheism: ﴿Praise﴾, that is, the comprehensive ascription of all attributes of perfection, ﴿belongs to God﴾, who has no equal and to whom no one else has any comprehensive hold on anything at all. Thus the proof is binding on them by what they admitted of His comprehensiveness, while they do not affirm that by turning away from it. ﴿But most of them do not reason﴾ [that is: no intellect is renewed for them; some of them absolutely, because he died a disbeliever], since they acknowledge the meaning of praise, that He is the Creator of everything, at the beginning and in restoration, and yet they do what contradicts that, associating others with Him, whom they themselves acknowledge He created, and they do not put their trust in Him in all affairs, on land and at sea, and they do not direct worship purely to Him. Thus they do not understand the meaning of praise, since they do not act upon it. [And some of them believed after that and were at the summit of perfection of intellect in monotheism, which is followed by all the branches; and some of them were below that, so the negation of knowledge from them was qualified by perfection.]

When these verses have made clear that the world is founded on perishing and passing away, on abandonment and departure, and it is established that rejoicing in it is misplaced, Allah the Exalted therefore said, pointing (after stripping them of intellect) to the fact that they are in it like beasts that rut openly: ﴿And what is this worldly life﴾. So He belittled it by the demonstrative and by the term of lowliness (al-dana'ah), with an indication that acknowledging this name suffices to compel acknowledgment of the other life (the Hereafter).

Since the aim of the surah is to urge jihad and to forbid what is wrong, and since it is in the context of stripping them of intellect, He put forward diversion (al-lahw) first, because turning away from it cuts off the root of evil, for it is what drives people to it.
