So He said: ﴿nothing but diversion﴾, meaning a thing that distracts from what benefits, ﴿and play﴾ (al-la'ib), which occupies the children of the intellect and every heedless and ignorant person. For diversion is everything that by its nature pleases the soul, such as singing, adornment with wealth and women, and other things, through which joy and an increase of delight arise. It thus becomes a cause of heedlessness, distraction, forgetfulness and preoccupation, away from using the intellect to follow what saves one in the Hereafter, and from it arises error, as the verse of Luqman indicates: ﴿who buys idle talk to lead astray from the way of Allah﴾ [Luqman: 6]. From it comes play, which is doing what increases the soul's delight in this world, such as dancing after listening, and it ends quickly because it is the opposite of seriousness and resembles jesting. It is every base thing and every falsehood aimed at increasing expansion and recreation and indulging in passing time with what one desires without weariness. (The word la'bah, with a dammah, means an image, and anything played with, such as chess; the fool mocks with it. La'iba means he was merry; and in matters of religion, he treated it lightly.)

Since they denied life after death, He stated emphatically that there is no life other than this: ﴿And indeed the Last Abode, that is indeed the Life﴾, meaning specifically ﴿the Life﴾ (al-hayawan), that is, the complete, enduring, all-encompassing, and perfect life itself, in that there is no death in it and no perishing for anything. For this reason this pattern (fa'alan), which indicates intensification, was chosen; and its vowelling (haraka) suggests what life contains of mere movement and agitation. So there is no ending to any of its play, nor to its pleasures, which correspond to what is in this world only in form, not in meaning, for there is nothing base in it, neither in what moves to it nor in what it moves toward. Rather, its delight lies in glorification and sanctification and what follows from them of knowledge, expansion, recreation, openness, intimacy and gladness.

Since they [had] erred regarding both abodes, assigning each to a position other than its own, for they reckoned the world an enduring existence in this state, and the Hereafter a non-existence with no existence in any way, He said: ﴿If only they knew﴾, meaning [that is,] a condition that is like an innate nature, that they would have knowledge and would not have erred regarding either of them. Then they would not have persisted, despite their preference for life and their intense aversion to death, believing that there is no resurrection after it into the world, whereas its origin is the absence of life, which is the state of death.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 65:

When He concluded this verse with what implies that they do not know, and the preceding one with [the statement] that most of them do not reason, He made the following statement a consequence of that: ﴿So when﴾, i.e., as a result of their lack of reason, which necessarily entails their lack of knowledge, that when they ﴿board﴾, i.e., the sea, ﴿in the ship﴾, i.e., the ships, ﴿they call upon God﴾, i.e., the Sovereign, the Most High, who encompasses everything, whenever a calamity befalls them and they fear destruction from it, ﴿sincere﴾ in monotheism ﴿to Him in religion﴾, turning away from their associates in heart and tongue, because they are certain that in those dire straits there is no savior other than Him. ﴿Then when He delivers them﴾, i.e., God, glorified is He, bringing them ﴿safely to the land, behold, they﴾, i.e., at the moment of reaching the land, (p-477) ﴿associate [others with Him]﴾. Thus it is established that they do not know, because they do not reason, since they acknowledge the helplessness of their gods yet associate them with Him. In this there is the greatest mockery of them.

Al-Baghawi said: ʿIkrimah said: "When they boarded the sea, they carried the idols with them. When the wind grew fierce against them, they threw them into the sea and said, 'O Lord! O Lord!'"

Al-Razi said in al-Lawami': "This is evidence that knowledge of the Lord is in the innate nature (fitrah) of every human being, and that if they are heedless in times of ease, there is no doubt that they turn to Him in times of hardship." End of quote. Thus it is known that preoccupation with the worldly life is what blocks one from every good, and that detachment from it aids the original, upright fitrah. For this reason we find the poor closer to every good.

Since they were with this act, which none would commit except one whose reason has been taken away, claiming that they are the most intelligent of people and the most perceptive of the consequences of actions and of what disgraces men, and since their act was ingratitude for the blessing, while claiming that they are the most grateful of people for kindness, He said, explaining that their custom is contrary to the custom of the believers in [making the blessing of deliverance a cause for increasing their acts of obedience, so it is known that their sincerity at sea was only a form with no reality behind it]: ﴿That they may deny what We have given them﴾ of Our greatness in this blessing, whose greatness is sufficient in that no one other than Us can do it. They did not associate others with Us except for the sake of this denial; otherwise they would be doing something without purpose, and that would be the act of one who has no intellect at all, and they would be too proud for such a thing. ﴿And that they may enjoy themselves﴾ through what they gather together upon in associating partners with God, of mutual ties and cooperation. According to those who make the lam quiescent (sakkana al-lam), namely Ibn Kathir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Qalun from Nafi', it is conjoined (ma'tuf) as a threat, either to an implied clause, "so let them deny," or to the earlier ﴿that they may deny﴾, with its lam being the lam of command. What supports this will come in Surat al-Rum, God willing. ﴿But they will come to know﴾, by a promise that will not be broken, what will befall them through this act, which lies between disbelief and madness.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 67:

Since God, glorified is He, had granted them a vast and lasting security in the land, unlike the rest of the Arabs, which is the reverse of what was mentioned about their intense fear at sea, and since He was able to make them fear on land just as He was able to make them fear at sea, so that their sincerity might endure, and since their disbelief in the time of security after their sincerity in the time of fear (even though it is among the greatest of defects) is [frivolous] and is done only by one who has felt safe from such a calamity on land, the rebuke takes the form of saying: "Have they not seen that We are able to make them fear and to destroy them on land just as We are able to do so at sea, as We did to others?" So He follows it with His words: ﴿Have they not seen﴾ [i.e., ] with the eyes of their insight ﴿that We have made﴾ i.e., by Our greatness for them ﴿a sanctuary (ḥaram)﴾. He said, ﴿secure (āmin)﴾ because there is no fear for whoever enters it. Since security pervades everything within it, it is as though it is itself security. It is the sacred Ḥaram of Mecca, and its security necessitates monotheism and sincerity, out of desire for its continuation and fear of its ending, [just as fear at sea necessitated sincerity, out of fear of its continuation and desire for its ending]. And the situation is that ﴿they are snatched away (yatakhaṭṭafu)﴾. He used the passive form because the intended matter is the act itself, not a specific agent.

Since snatching away was not restricted to some people rather than others, but all the Arabs would raid one another and attack one another with killing, capture, plunder, and other kinds of harm, He said: ﴿the people around them﴾, i.e., around the one who is in it, from every direction, snatching away birds, despite the small number of those in Mecca and the large number of those around them. So the One who broke the customary pattern in acting this way, until it became as it is, is able to reverse the situation, making those in the Ḥaram the ones snatched away and those around it secure, or making all of them subject to fear in one uniform manner.

Since it has become clear that there is no basis for their associating partners with God or for their disbelief in this manifest and evident blessing, the rebuke is brought in His words: ﴿Then in falsehood (al-bāṭil)﴾, i.e., specifically in idols and other things, ﴿do they believe?﴾ while the situation is that no sensible person doubts its falsehood. The restriction (ḥaṣr) comes from the fact that whoever disbelieves in God is followed by disbelief in every truth and belief in every falsehood. ﴿And in the blessing of God﴾ which He brought about for them, namely deliverance and other things, ﴿they disbelieve﴾ [p. 480] in that they made the place of their gratitude to Him for deliverance into their associating others in worship with Him.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 68:

Since injustice (*ẓulm*) is placing a thing in other than its proper place, and placing a thing in a place that cannot receive it is the most unjust (*aẓlam*) form of injustice, their act, which is attributing to what knows nothing and has no power over anything a station that belongs to One who knows everything and has power over everything, is the most unjust of injustices. So the sense is: "Who is more unjust than them in this?" He connected to it His words: ﴿And who is more unjust﴾, meaning: who is more severe in placing things in other than their proper places, because he has no light but is in the darkness of ignorance, groping. ﴿than one who fabricates against God a lie﴾, meaning: deliberately does so, ﴿any lie whatsoever﴾, meaning: any lie at all, whether shirk or otherwise, as they used to say when they committed an indecency: "We found our fathers doing it, and God commanded us to it." ﴿or denies the truth﴾, meaning this Qur'an, which is miraculous and clear, conveyed through this trustworthy Messenger, who never reported a report except that reality corresponded to it, ﴿when it comes to him﴾, meaning: when it comes to him, ﴿without delay﴾, that he may look and reflect upon what has come to him of this serious and dangerous matter.

Since the implied sense is: "No one is more unjust than him; rather he is the most unjust of the unjust, so he is a disbeliever, and his abode is Hell," and it was known that they would say out of obstinacy, "The matter is not so," He said, as a rebuke to them, and because their act is the act of one who denies, and as an affirmation to them, because when the interrogative *hamzat al-inkār* (the interrogative particle of denial) enters upon a negation it becomes an affirmation. He counted it, by this, as being in the position of what (p-481) has no dispute at all: ﴿Is there not in Hell an abode?﴾, meaning: a dwelling, a place of residence and confinement for him, although he has committed this great disbelief. This was the original form, but for the purpose of generality and linking the judgment to the attribute, He said: ﴿for the disbelievers﴾, meaning: those who cover up the lights of the manifest truth. Or (the sense is): "Is he not among the disbelievers?" That is: each of the two premises is correct and undeniable, and their denial cannot be coherent except by corrupting one of them. As for his disbelief in the Benefactor after He saved him from destruction, by worshipping other than Him, no intelligent person can deny it. And as for the fact that Hell contains him after the One who has power has informed of it, no one who affirms power can deny it. So the two premises are things about which there is no objection in their view, and they yield the conclusion that his abode is Hell. [The syllogism (*qiyās*, logical analogy) takes this form: "One who worships other than the One who saved him is a disbeliever, and every disbeliever's abode is Hell; therefore the one who worships other than the One who saved him has Hell as his abode."]

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 29, verse 69:

Since all of this concerns those who were tested and did not struggle against their souls, the meaning is: those whom We tested and found to be liars went astray, and so they became people who do not reason and do not know, because they were not among the strugglers. Thus He conjoined to it His saying: ﴿And those who strive﴾, meaning: those who exerted jihad (striving) to the utmost of their effort, as indicated by the form of the verb (mufa'alah). ﴿in Us﴾, meaning: for the sake of Our right and out of Our watchfulness, specifically by holding fast to acts of obedience, through jihad against the disbelievers and others (p-482) and in every matter in which striving is fitting, by word and deed, in hardship and ease, and by opposing desire at the onset of trials and severe afflictions, keeping Our greatness in mind.

Since the disbelievers deny their own success, and since the one who succeeds and prevails in everything is the one who is guided, He said, using the cause to express the effect: ﴿We will surely guide them﴾ to what We grant them of the light which does not let astray whoever accompanies it, a guidance befitting Our greatness, ﴿Our ways﴾, meaning: there are no ways other than them, in knowledge and in action, and We will be with them by Our kindness and Our help, because they excelled in striving. So blessed is whoever fights in the way of God even for the span of a milking of a she-camel, on account of this verse and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who are killed in the way of God, He will not let their deeds go astray﴾ [Muhammad: 4] ﴿He will guide them and set right their condition﴾ [Muhammad: 5]. For this reason Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah used to say: When people disagree, look at what the people of raiding (ghazw) hold to.

Since the one who does good (muhsin), whenever his share in the station of ihsan (excellence in worship and conduct) increases, his share of this world decreases, the foolish conclude that God has no care for him. He therefore magnified the emphasis in His saying, [turning the speech away from the style of majesty to a style more excellent for it, with what it adds of beauty]: ﴿Indeed, God﴾, meaning: with His greatness, majesty, grandeur, and all His perfection, ﴿is surely with﴾ them. This was the original form, but He intended to inform of their excellence and to attach the judgment to the attribute and to generalize, so He made it explicit, saying: ﴿with the good-doers﴾, meaning: all of them, with victory and help in their worldly life, and reward and forgiveness in their afterlife, on account of their striving, because it is gratitude, and gratitude calls for increase. Whoever is with Him, glorified is He, attains every sought goal, even if the ignorant one sees otherwise. He makes their might come from behind humiliation and conceals their richness under the cover of poverty, as a protection for them from what constant might drags toward, which is arrogance, and what great wealth drives toward, which is tyranny. How well Abu al-Qasim al-Qushayri, the Ustadh, conveyed in al-Risalah from al-Harith al-Muhasibi that he said: Whoever sets right his inward through watchfulness (muraqabah) and sincerity (ikhlas), God adorns his outward through striving and following the Sunnah (the prophetic practice).

The verse is an instance of ihtibak (a device in which two elements are each mentioned and each implies the omission of the other): it first mentions striving as evidence for its omission the second time, and secondly mentions being with the good-doers as evidence for the omission of being with (Him) and of excellence the first time. Thus the beginning of the surah embraces this ending, and it was the greatest observer of it. So we ask God for well-being from trials, and for striving if there must be ordeals. And to Him is the return.
